Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ) quietly disclosed a number that changes the scale of its OpenAI relationship. In its fiscal 2026 10-K, Microsoft said it recorded $24.1 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments. It also had $6.0 billion of accounts receivable from OpenAI at June 30. The number is huge. The missing number may be even more consequential. For investors trying to decide whether the AI buildout is producing returns or merely moving cash among strategic partners, the distinction between revenue scale and margin quality is the whole story.

Microsoft does not separately disclose the profit generated by those OpenAI commercial arrangements. The $24.1 billion should not be confused with pure Azure revenue or treated as a clean measure of AI cloud sales. It includes the economics created by the companies' broader partnership, while Microsoft also owns an around 25% interest in OpenAI on an as-converted basis and continues to receive revenue-sharing payments.

The strategic logic is still powerful, because Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) funds and supplies infrastructure to one of the largest AI labs, gets access to OpenAI intellectual property for its products, sells cloud capacity into the relationship and participates financially in OpenAI's growth. Fiscal 2026 Microsoft Cloud growth helped push total company revenue up 18%, and Microsoft recorded $5.0 billion of net-income benefit from net gains on its OpenAI investments.

But the 10-K also shows why investors should resist treating every OpenAI dollar as high-margin software revenue. Microsoft Cloud gross margin fell to 66%, with management citing continued AI-infrastructure investment and growing AI product usage. Costs are arriving alongside the revenue through data centers, server components, depreciation and financing structures. The OpenAI relationship can be extraordinarily valuable while still carrying economics that differ sharply from Microsoft's traditional software franchise. That gap is precisely why the disclosed revenue deserves analysis instead of automatic celebration.

Insider Monkey's database showed 273 hedge funds holding MSFT as of Q2, down from 282 in Q1. Those filings precede the annual report's full-year disclosure. As of August 14, roughly 68.54 million Microsoft shares were sold short, about 0.92% of the public float, with 2.1 days to cover. The $24.1 billion figure answers whether OpenAI is already financially material to Microsoft. It does not answer the more important valuation question: how much incremental profit Microsoft keeps after paying for the infrastructure and capital required to produce it.

sources.title: OpenAI hits $10 billion in annual recurring revenue fueled by ChatGPT growth - CNBC
passages: OpenAI has hit $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, or ARR, less than three years after launching its popular ChatGPT chatbot.
WATCH: OpenAI paying business users of ChatGPT hits 3 million, up from 2 million in February
For all of last year, OpenAI had around $5.5 billion in ARR.
Reaching its meteoric growth rates requires a substantial amount of cash.
OpenAI is also targeting $125 billion in revenue by 2029, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are confidential.
The Information first reported on OpenAI's revenue ambitions.
The new revenue metrics give some context to OpenAI's monster valuation.
OpenAI closed a $40 billion funding round in March, marking the largest private tech deal on record.
At today's metrics, OpenAI is valued at about 30 times revenue, which highlights the hyper growth expectations by some of its largest investors.
OpenAI is backed by Japan's SoftBank , Microsoft , Coatue, Altimeter, Thrive and others.
The figure includes sales from the company's consumer products; ChatGPT business products; and its application programming interface, or API.
It excludes licensing revenue from Microsoft and large one-time deals, according to an OpenAI spokesperson.
OpenAI burst onto the scene with the release of the consumer version of ChatGPT in late 2022, and began launching business products the following year.
As of late March, OpenAI said it supports 500 million weekly active users.

sources.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
passages: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday.

That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers .
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion.
At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June.
That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.
TechCrunch has reached out for more information.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers.
In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September.
That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization.
Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

sources.title: Microsoft’s $3.2 Billion Anthropic Score Dwarfs OpenAI in Blockbuster Quarter - finance.biggo.com
passages: On an annual basis, the two bets aren’t far apart: OpenAI contributed $5 billion over 12 months, while Anthropic delivered $3.2 billion in just three months.
The takeaway for investors is that Microsoft has diversified its AI exposure beyond a single lab, and the newer bet is already proving its worth.
That single-quarter contribution accounted for nearly 7% of the company’s total diluted EPS of $4.81.

The disclosure marks the first time Microsoft has broken out Anthropic’s impact as an investment gain, though the AI lab had appeared in prior earnings calls as a major Azure customer and model supplier.
Note: Microsoft’s release attributes the roughly 7-cent Q4 EPS drag to a $600 million markdown embedded within the quarter — a sub-component of the period’s net $480 million gain.
The gap illustrates how equity-method accounting for a private stake like OpenAI’s can bundle several offsetting valuation events into a single quarter.
It closed a $30 billion round in February at a $380 billion valuation, then raised another $65 billion just over three months later, pushing its valuation to $965 billion.

While the AI investment narrative has shifted from “how much are you spending” to “what are you earning,” Microsoft’s results suggest the answer is increasingly “both.” By backing Anthropic and OpenAI simultaneously, the company has positioned itself to capture value regardless of which lab leads the next model cycle — all while both competitors pour money back into Azure.
Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 full-year revenue reached $331.8 billion, with net income of $133.7 billion.
The company added 31 new data centers across five continents in the quarter, bringing the calendar-year total to 88.
Microsoft executives made clear that the infrastructure spending spree is far from over.
Quarterly capital expenditures soared 70% to $41 billion, with roughly two-thirds going toward short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs.
The windfall traces back to November 2025, when Microsoft and Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) struck a three-way deal with Anthropic.
The arrangement effectively recycles capital: Microsoft invests, Anthropic spends the money on Azure, and Nvidia supplies the chips.
OpenAI’s contribution, by comparison, looked erratic.
Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI and accounts for the investment under new rules tied to the startup’s capital restructuring.

Instead of simply reflecting OpenAI’s operating results, Microsoft now books gains or losses based on changes in its share of OpenAI’s net assets — a formula that swings wildly with each funding round, valuation shift, or equity dilution.
That mechanical quirk produced a wild ride over the past year: a $3.1 billion net loss in fiscal Q1, a $7.6 billion gain in Q2, a $14 million loss in Q3, and a $480 million net gain in Q4.
For the latest quarter, OpenAI reduced diluted EPS by about 7 cents.
For the September quarter, Microsoft expects total revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion.
“We are advancing the frontier on the cost-to-outcome curve, ensuring every customer can turn tokens into business results,” Nadella said in a statement.
The after-hours rally signaled that Microsoft cleared the bar that Alphabet failed to meet a week earlier.

Google Cloud revenue had surged 82% to $24.8 billion, but Alphabet shares plunged as much as 7% after the company raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion-$205 billion, up from a prior $180 billion-$190 billion range.
Investors feared the bill was growing faster than the payoff.
Microsoft faced the same test and got the opposite verdict.
“This report reminded investors that it is also becoming one of the largest monetizers of AI.”
Microsoft’s stock had been the second-worst performer in the Magnificent Seven this year, down about 19% through Tuesday’s close.
The earnings beat and maintained capex guidance appeared to reset expectations.
Overall Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 27% to $59.3 billion.

The software and cloud giant reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $90 billion, up 18% from a year earlier and well above Wall Street estimates of $87.7 billion. Net income surged 31% to $35.8 billion. Adjusted earnings hit $4.74 per share, crushing the consensus forecast of $4.24. The stock jumped roughly 9% in extended trading Wednesday, a sharp contrast to the selloff that greeted Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL) after its own cloud blowout a week earlier.

Microsoft executives made clear that the infrastructure spending spree is far from over. Quarterly capital expenditures soared 70% to $41 billion, with roughly two-thirds going toward short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs. CFO Amy Hood said the company expects capex to climb above $50 billion next quarter, and the full-year outlook for calendar 2026 stands at about $175 billion — a figure comparable to the $190 billion forecast issued in April after adjusting for changes in the estimated useful life of data centers and office buildings.
Yet for the first time, investors got a detailed look at how Microsoft’s dual-track AI investment strategy is playing out — and the contrast was stark.

Microsoft recorded a $3.2 billion gain on its Anthropic stake in the quarter ended June 30, adding roughly 33 cents to diluted earnings per share. That single-quarter contribution accounted for nearly 7% of the company’s total diluted EPS of $4.81. The disclosure marks the first time Microsoft has broken out Anthropic’s impact as an investment gain, though the AI lab had appeared in prior earnings calls as a major Azure customer and model supplier.

The windfall traces back to November 2025, when Microsoft and Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) struck a three-way deal with Anthropic. Microsoft committed up to $5 billion, Nvidia up to $10 billion, and Anthropic agreed to buy $30 billion in Azure computing services while planning to add up to 1 gigawatt of compute capacity. The arrangement effectively recycles capital: Microsoft invests, Anthropic spends the money on Azure, and Nvidia supplies the chips.
The circular flow of capital and hardware can be summarized as follows:

Anthropic’s valuation has skyrocketed since. It closed a $30 billion round in February at a $380 billion valuation, then raised another $65 billion just over three months later, pushing its valuation to $965 billion. That rapid markup — more than 2.5 times in a single quarter — is what flowed through to Microsoft’s bottom line.

OpenAI’s contribution, by comparison, looked erratic. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI and accounts for the investment under new rules tied to the startup’s capital restructuring. Instead of simply reflecting OpenAI’s operating results, Microsoft now books gains or losses based on changes in its share of OpenAI’s net assets — a formula that swings wildly with each funding round, valuation shift, or equity dilution.

That mechanical quirk produced a wild ride over the past year: a $3.1 billion net loss in fiscal Q1, a $7.6 billion gain in Q2, a $14 million loss in Q3, and a $480 million net gain in Q4. For the latest quarter, OpenAI reduced diluted EPS by about 7 cents. For the full fiscal year, however, the investment generated a $5 billion gain and added 67 cents to EPS.

Note: Microsoft’s release attributes the roughly 7-cent Q4 EPS drag to a $600 million markdown embedded within the quarter — a sub-component of the period’s net $480 million gain. The gap illustrates how equity-method accounting for a private stake like OpenAI’s can bundle several offsetting valuation events into a single quarter.

On an annual basis, the two bets aren’t far apart: OpenAI contributed $5 billion over 12 months, while Anthropic delivered $3.2 billion in just three months. The takeaway for investors is that Microsoft has diversified its AI exposure beyond a single lab, and the newer bet is already proving its worth.

Beyond the investment ledger, the operating results gave bulls plenty to cheer. Azure revenue jumped 43% year-over-year, the fastest growth in four years and more than 3 percentage points above the roughly 40% analysts had expected. Overall Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 27% to $59.3 billion.

CEO Satya Nadella said Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time in the fiscal year, while Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats. “We are advancing the frontier on the cost-to-outcome curve, ensuring every customer can turn tokens into business results,” Nadella said in a statement.

The company guided for Azure growth to accelerate again next quarter to roughly 45%, even as capex rises. Hood noted that new capacity is generating revenue almost immediately: “When we can make efficiency gains, they are quickly monetized in quarter.”

The after-hours rally signaled that Microsoft cleared the bar that Alphabet failed to meet a week earlier. Google Cloud revenue had surged 82% to $24.8 billion, but Alphabet shares plunged as much as 7% after the company raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion-$205 billion, up from a prior $180 billion-$190 billion range. Investors feared the bill was growing faster than the payoff.

Microsoft faced the same test and got the opposite verdict. “After months of questions about the company’s infrastructure spending, the quarter showed that those investments are increasingly translating into revenue growth, backlog expansion and Copilot adoption,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion. “This report reminded investors that it is also becoming one of the largest monetizers of AI.”

Microsoft’s stock had been the second-worst performer in the Magnificent Seven this year, down about 19% through Tuesday’s close. The earnings beat and maintained capex guidance appeared to reset expectations.

Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 full-year revenue reached $331.8 billion, with net income of $133.7 billion. The company added 31 new data centers across five continents in the quarter, bringing the calendar-year total to 88.

While the AI investment narrative has shifted from “how much are you spending” to “what are you earning,” Microsoft’s results suggest the answer is increasingly “both.” By backing Anthropic and OpenAI simultaneously, the company has positioned itself to capture value regardless of which lab leads the next model cycle — all while both competitors pour money back into Azure.

For the September quarter, Microsoft expects total revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion. The company said its calendar 2026 capex expectations remain unchanged from the updated $175 billion figure, reflecting a change in the estimated useful life of data centers and office buildings rather than a reduction in actual spending.

sources.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
passages: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday.

That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers .
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion.
At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June.
That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.
TechCrunch has reached out for more information.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers.
In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September.
That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization.
Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

sources.title: Microsoft’s $3.2 Billion Anthropic Score Dwarfs OpenAI in Blockbuster Quarter - finance.biggo.com
passages: On an annual basis, the two bets aren’t far apart: OpenAI contributed $5 billion over 12 months, while Anthropic delivered $3.2 billion in just three months.
The takeaway for investors is that Microsoft has diversified its AI exposure beyond a single lab, and the newer bet is already proving its worth.
That single-quarter contribution accounted for nearly 7% of the company’s total diluted EPS of $4.81.

The disclosure marks the first time Microsoft has broken out Anthropic’s impact as an investment gain, though the AI lab had appeared in prior earnings calls as a major Azure customer and model supplier.
Note: Microsoft’s release attributes the roughly 7-cent Q4 EPS drag to a $600 million markdown embedded within the quarter — a sub-component of the period’s net $480 million gain.
The gap illustrates how equity-method accounting for a private stake like OpenAI’s can bundle several offsetting valuation events into a single quarter.
It closed a $30 billion round in February at a $380 billion valuation, then raised another $65 billion just over three months later, pushing its valuation to $965 billion.

While the AI investment narrative has shifted from “how much are you spending” to “what are you earning,” Microsoft’s results suggest the answer is increasingly “both.” By backing Anthropic and OpenAI simultaneously, the company has positioned itself to capture value regardless of which lab leads the next model cycle — all while both competitors pour money back into Azure.
Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 full-year revenue reached $331.8 billion, with net income of $133.7 billion.
The company added 31 new data centers across five continents in the quarter, bringing the calendar-year total to 88.
Microsoft executives made clear that the infrastructure spending spree is far from over.
Quarterly capital expenditures soared 70% to $41 billion, with roughly two-thirds going toward short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs.
The windfall traces back to November 2025, when Microsoft and Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) struck a three-way deal with Anthropic.
The arrangement effectively recycles capital: Microsoft invests, Anthropic spends the money on Azure, and Nvidia supplies the chips.
OpenAI’s contribution, by comparison, looked erratic.
Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI and accounts for the investment under new rules tied to the startup’s capital restructuring.

Instead of simply reflecting OpenAI’s operating results, Microsoft now books gains or losses based on changes in its share of OpenAI’s net assets — a formula that swings wildly with each funding round, valuation shift, or equity dilution.
That mechanical quirk produced a wild ride over the past year: a $3.1 billion net loss in fiscal Q1, a $7.6 billion gain in Q2, a $14 million loss in Q3, and a $480 million net gain in Q4.
For the latest quarter, OpenAI reduced diluted EPS by about 7 cents.
For the September quarter, Microsoft expects total revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion.
“We are advancing the frontier on the cost-to-outcome curve, ensuring every customer can turn tokens into business results,” Nadella said in a statement.
The after-hours rally signaled that Microsoft cleared the bar that Alphabet failed to meet a week earlier.

Google Cloud revenue had surged 82% to $24.8 billion, but Alphabet shares plunged as much as 7% after the company raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion-$205 billion, up from a prior $180 billion-$190 billion range.
Investors feared the bill was growing faster than the payoff.
Microsoft faced the same test and got the opposite verdict.
“This report reminded investors that it is also becoming one of the largest monetizers of AI.”
Microsoft’s stock had been the second-worst performer in the Magnificent Seven this year, down about 19% through Tuesday’s close.
The earnings beat and maintained capex guidance appeared to reset expectations.
Overall Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 27% to $59.3 billion.

(MSFT) just delivered its strongest evidence yet that the AI spending spree is paying off, but the real stunner was buried inside the earnings: a $3.2 billion gain from its bet on Anthropic in a single quarter, completely overshadowing the roller-coaster returns from its much larger, longer-standing alliance with OpenAI. The software and cloud giant reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $90 billion, up 18% from a year earlier and well above Wall Street estimates of $87.7 billion. Net income surged 31% to $35.8 billion. Adjusted earnings hit $4.74 per share, crushing the consensus forecast of $4.24. The stock jumped roughly 9% in extended trading Wednesday, a sharp contrast to the selloff that greeted Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL) after its own cloud blowout a week earlier. Microsoft executives made clear that the infrastructure spending spree is far from over. Quarterly capital expenditures soared 70% to $41 billion, with roughly two-thirds going toward short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs. CFO Amy Hood said the company expects capex to climb above $50 billion next quarter, and the full-year outlook for calendar 2026 stands at about $175 billion — a figure comparable to the $190 billion forecast issued in April after adjusting for changes in the estimated useful life of data centers and office buildings. Yet for the first time, investors got a detailed look at how Microsoft’s dual-track AI investment strategy is playing out — and the contrast was stark. Microsoft recorded a $3.2 billion gain on its Anthropic stake in the quarter ended June 30, adding roughly 33 cents to diluted earnings per share. That single-quarter contribution accounted for nearly 7% of the company’s total diluted EPS of $4.81. The disclosure marks the first time Microsoft has broken out Anthropic’s impact as an investment gain, though the AI lab had appeared in prior earnings calls as a major Azure customer and model supplier. The windfall traces back to November 2025, when Microsoft and Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) struck a three-way deal with Anthropic. Microsoft committed up to $5 billion, Nvidia up to $10 billion, and Anthropic agreed to buy $30 billion in Azure computing services while planning to add up to 1 gigawatt of compute capacity. The arrangement effectively recycles capital: Microsoft invests, Anthropic spends the money on Azure, and Nvidia supplies the chips. It closed a $30 billion round in February at a $380 billion valuation, then raised another $65 billion just over three months later, pushing its valuation to $965 billion. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI and accounts for the investment under new rules tied to the startup’s capital restructuring. Instead of simply reflecting OpenAI’s operating results, Microsoft now books gains or losses based on changes in its share of OpenAI’s net assets — a formula that swings wildly with each funding round, valuation shift, or equity dilution. The gap illustrates how equity-method accounting for a private stake like OpenAI’s can bundle several offsetting valuation events into a single quarter. Azure revenue jumped 43% year-over-year, the fastest growth in four years and more than 3 percentage points above the roughly 40% analysts had expected. The windfall traces back to November 2025, when Microsoft and Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) struck a three-way deal with Anthropic. Microsoft committed up to $5 billion, Nvidia up to $10 billion, and Anthropic agreed to buy $30 billion in Azure computing services while planning to add up to 1 gigawatt of compute capacity. The arrangement effectively recycles capital: Microsoft invests, Anthropic spends the money on Azure, and Nvidia supplies the chips.
The circular flow of capital and hardware can be summarized as follows:

Anthropic’s valuation has skyrocketed since. It closed a $30 billion round in February at a $380 billion valuation, then raised another $65 billion just over three months later, pushing its valuation to $965 billion. That rapid markup — more than 2.5 times in a single quarter — is what flowed through to Microsoft’s bottom line.

OpenAI’s contribution, by comparison, looked erratic. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI and accounts for the investment under new rules tied to the startup’s capital restructuring. Instead of simply reflecting OpenAI’s operating results, Microsoft now books gains or losses based on changes in its share of OpenAI’s net assets — a formula that swings wildly with each funding round, valuation shift, or equity dilution.

That mechanical quirk produced a wild ride over the past year: a $3.1 billion net loss in fiscal Q1, a $7.6 billion gain in Q2, a $14 million loss in Q3, and a $480 million net gain in Q4. For the latest quarter, OpenAI reduced diluted EPS by about 7 cents. For the full fiscal year, however, the investment generated a $5 billion gain and added 67 cents to EPS.

Note: Microsoft’s release attributes the roughly 7-cent Q4 EPS drag to a $600 million markdown embedded within the quarter — a sub-component of the period’s net $480 million gain. The gap illustrates how equity-method accounting for a private stake like OpenAI’s can bundle several offsetting valuation events into a single quarter.

On an annual basis, the two bets aren’t far apart: OpenAI contributed $5 billion over 12 months, while Anthropic delivered $3.2 billion in just three months. The takeaway for investors is that Microsoft has diversified its AI exposure beyond a single lab, and the newer bet is already proving its worth.

Beyond the investment ledger, the operating results gave bulls plenty to cheer. Azure revenue jumped 43% year-over-year, the fastest growth in four years and more than 3 percentage points above the roughly 40% analysts had expected. Overall Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 27% to $59.3 billion.

CEO Satya Nadella said Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time in the fiscal year, while Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats. “We are advancing the frontier on the cost-to-outcome curve, ensuring every customer can turn tokens into business results,” Nadella said in a statement.

The company guided for Azure growth to accelerate again next quarter to roughly 45%, even as capex rises. Hood noted that new capacity is generating revenue almost immediately: “When we can make efficiency gains, they are quickly monetized in quarter.”

The after-hours rally signaled that Microsoft cleared the bar that Alphabet failed to meet a week earlier. Google Cloud revenue had surged 82% to $24.8 billion, but Alphabet shares plunged as much as 7% after the company raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion-$205 billion, up from a prior $180 billion-$190 billion range. Investors feared the bill was growing faster than the payoff.

Microsoft faced the same test and got the opposite verdict. “After months of questions about the company’s infrastructure spending, the quarter showed that those investments are increasingly translating into revenue growth, backlog expansion and Copilot adoption,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion. “This report reminded investors that it is also becoming one of the largest monetizers of AI.”

Microsoft’s stock had been the second-worst performer in the Magnificent Seven this year, down about 19% through Tuesday’s close. The earnings beat and maintained capex guidance appeared to reset expectations.

Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 full-year revenue reached $331.8 billion, with net income of $133.7 billion. The company added 31 new data centers across five continents in the quarter, bringing the calendar-year total to 88.

While the AI investment narrative has shifted from “how much are you spending” to “what are you earning,” Microsoft’s results suggest the answer is increasingly “both.” By backing Anthropic and OpenAI simultaneously, the company has positioned itself to capture value regardless of which lab leads the next model cycle — all while both competitors pour money back into Azure.

For the September quarter, Microsoft expects total revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion. The company said its calendar 2026 capex expectations remain unchanged from the updated $175 billion figure, reflecting a change in the estimated useful life of data centers and office buildings rather than a reduction in actual spending.

sources.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon Promises 'Significant Leap' In AI Coding And Cybersecurity - Engadget
passages: OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier models have been trading blows of late, with each claiming bragging rights in different categories.
Now, Google has barged in with its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model, boasting of top benchmark scores in key areas like cybersecurity and coding.
"Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we're pushing the frontier forward," the company wrote in a blog post .
Google also claims a near sweep across categories including agentic coding, computer use, knowledge work, science and math, and others.
Google especially highlighted Carbon's domination in cybersecurity, where it bested other models by fairly wide margins.

The company said that it also advances frontier model safety and security by reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation, boosting transparency and honesty (yes, there's a test for "unsupported claims"), resisting prompt injection, improving collaboration and "following through without overstepping." It's also twice as likely to generate secure code compared to Argon.
As we've seen with previous frontier models, Carbon will only be released to select cybersecurity defense companies at first, to allow for pre-release model testing.
Google will eventually allow access to additional trusted partners through the company's Fairwind Program, before releasing it widely.

sources.title: Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model - blog.google
passages: Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.
In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report .
With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.
Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment.
We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding.
With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena .
Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense.
On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon.
As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches.
Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.
Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59.
We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing.
Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows.

Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

sources.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can’t use - Ars Technica
passages: It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year.
Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon .
This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon.
Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models.
Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
In the Grey Swan evaluation, Carbon resisted every attempted prompt-injection attack.
That 0 percent score is better than Argon (0.7 percent), Opus 5.5 (1 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (8.5 percent).
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts.
Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it.
Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests.
The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.
Carbon will probably arrive first for AI Ultra subscribers and developers using the Gemini API.
Like Argon, Google will temporarily offer a discounted API rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
That price will double once the introductory period expires.
Argon’s discounted rates are only good through the end of November, but Google doesn’t specify a date for Carbon.
Google has declined to provide an end date when asked, suggesting it hasn’t decided when the price will increase.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis.
It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.

coreStoryFacts.text: There are “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity defense (finding vulnerabilities).
Notably, “Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59.”
Based on user feedback following the last launch, Google worked to improve Carbon across “coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding.”
Following the launch of Argon two weeks ago, Google today announced Gemini 4 Carbon as its next frontier model.

Once available, Google will offer introductory pricing of “$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.” Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.
Google says this fast release is due to its researchers and models “working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster.”
Interested in the minutiae of Google and Alphabet.
OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier models have been trading blows of late, with each claiming bragging rights in different categories.
Now, Google has barged in with its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model, boasting of top benchmark scores in key areas like cybersecurity and coding.
"Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we're pushing the frontier forward," the company wrote in a blog post .
Google also claims a near sweep across categories including agentic coding, computer use, knowledge work, science and math, and others.
Google especially highlighted Carbon's domination in cybersecurity, where it bested other models by fairly wide margins.

The company said that it also advances frontier model safety and security by reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation, boosting transparency and honesty (yes, there's a test for "unsupported claims"), resisting prompt injection, improving collaboration and "following through without overstepping." It's also twice as likely to generate secure code compared to Argon.
As we've seen with previous frontier models, Carbon will only be released to select cybersecurity defense companies at first, to allow for pre-release model testing.
Google will eventually allow access to additional trusted partners through the company's Fairwind Program, before releasing it widely.

passages: It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year.
Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon .
This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon.
Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models.
Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
In the Grey Swan evaluation, Carbon resisted every attempted prompt-injection attack.
That 0 percent score is better than Argon (0.7 percent), Opus 5.5 (1 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (8.5 percent).
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts.
Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it.
Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests.
The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.
Carbon will probably arrive first for AI Ultra subscribers and developers using the Gemini API.
Like Argon, Google will temporarily offer a discounted API rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
That price will double once the introductory period expires.
Argon’s discounted rates are only good through the end of November, but Google doesn’t specify a date for Carbon.
Google has declined to provide an end date when asked, suggesting it hasn’t decided when the price will increase.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis.
It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.
Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information.
After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena .

Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.

Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.

In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.

Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

sources.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
passages: It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year.
Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon .
This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon.
Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models.
Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
In the Grey Swan evaluation, Carbon resisted every attempted prompt-injection attack.
That 0 percent score is better than Argon (0.7 percent), Opus 5.5 (1 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (8.5 percent).
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts.
Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it.
Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests.
The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.
Carbon will probably arrive first for AI Ultra subscribers and developers using the Gemini API.
Like Argon, Google will temporarily offer a discounted API rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
That price will double once the introductory period expires.
Argon’s discounted rates are only good through the end of November, but Google doesn’t specify a date for Carbon.
Google has declined to provide an end date when asked, suggesting it hasn’t decided when the price will increase.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis.
It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.

The post points to cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks, meaning complicated jobs that take many steps or run for a long time, as Carbon’s biggest strengths. Already, Gemini 4 Carbon has the top spot in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, beating out Claude Opus 5.5. Credit: Screenshot: Artificial Analysis SEE ALSO: Google says Gemini 4 Argon agents beat 'Minecraft' without human help The pace at which AI companies are releasing new frontier models has accelerated sharply in recent months, as the frontier AI labs race to have the best model available. 22, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra earlier that month, and Google announced Argon on Sept. 30 before releasing it to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers on Oct. Each lab has claimed a new lead within weeks of the last.As with Argon, Google is announcing Carbon well before most people can use it. Carbon is starting with a small group of cybersecurity defenders, and Google hasn’t said when it will reach everyone else. (Last week's PHP2Shell incident shows just how much havoc new AI models could wreak on the internet at large.) Announcing early lets Google claim the top spot on the leaderboards now. It also gives everyone a look at the benchmarks before the next round of releases.Gemini 4 Carbon: BenchmarksIn Google’s comparison table, Carbon posts the top score on 15 of 17 benchmarks against Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1. All figures in this section are as reported by Google. Credit: Google The two benchmarks Carbon doesn’t win are worth noting. Claude Opus 5.5 leads on OSWorld-2.1, which measures how well a model can operate a computer.A big change from Argon is that Google now reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 scores run by Artificial Analysis, an independent testing firm, rather than its own. For quick context, Terminal-Bench 4.0 measures how well an AI model can complete real technical tasks — like installing software or fixing broken code — by typing commands into a computer’s terminal on its own. It's one of the hardest agentic tests for LLMs.This is notable because the scores companies reported for each other’s models didn’t always line up with independent testing. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Carbon jumps about eight points over Argon and moves ahead of Opus 5.5.Google also says Carbon can work on difficult engineering problems for days at a time. Artificial Analysis runs a range of tests itself and combines them into a single composite score.On the newly updated version 5.0, Carbon (high) scores 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max). Gemini 4 Carbon's score of 59 is leaps above Argon's 50. Credit: Artificial Analysis The scores can’t be directly compared to the previous version of the index, where Argon (High) scored 53. A one-point lead is also thin enough that the next release from OpenAI or Anthropic could easily erase it. Carbon and Meta’s Muse Wonder Full are both flagged on the leaderboard as having no publicly available API, so they can’t yet be used outside their companies’ own access programs.Gemini 4 Carbon: Safety and safeguardsGoogle says Carbon uses the same safety system as Argon, which includes monitoring the model’s reasoning, and adds more work on alignment, or keeping the model behaving as intended. According to Google’s own testing, Carbon is also better behaved than its predecessor. Google says Carbon never successfully cheated on Terminal-Bench 4.0, meaning it never found a shortcut that passed a task without actually doing the work, and it tried to cheat only 0.4 percent of the time. During internal coding work, high-severity misalignment alerts, which flag a model acting in ways its developers didn’t intend, dropped by nearly 80 percent. Carbon also makes about half as many unsupported claims as Argon. And on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark, which tests whether hidden instructions can hijack a model, Carbon blocked every attack attempt, improving on Argon’s 0.7 percent attack success rate.All of these figures come from Google’s own testing.How to try Gemini 4 CarbonFor now, you can’t use Gemini 4 Carbon unless you’re an approved cyber defender in Google’s Fairwind Program. Starting this week, Carbon is rolling out to a small group of those testers, and Google says it will gradually add more trusted partners. Developers, businesses, and consumers will get access after that, but Google hasn’t given an exact public launch date.If we use Argon to figure out a timeline, about two weeks passed between its announcement and its arrival in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers. Though we won't be able to confirm whether Google will commit to that same schedule for Carbon.When Carbon does reach the API, Google says it will cost the same as Argon’s introductory price:$2 per million input tokens$10 per million output tokensCached input tokens at 95 percent off the input priceThat keeps Carbon well below its main rivals.

Though we won't be able to confirm whether Google will commit to that same schedule for Carbon.When Carbon does reach the API, Google says it will cost the same as Argon’s introductory price:$2 per million input tokens$10 per million output tokensCached input tokens at 95 percent off the input priceThat keeps Carbon well below its main rivals.

Carbon is starting with a small group of cybersecurity defenders, and Google hasn’t said when it will reach everyone else. (Last week's PHP2Shell incident shows just how much havoc new AI models could wreak on the internet at large.) Announcing early lets Google claim the top spot on the leaderboards now.

28, Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind, the company’s frontier AI lab, called Carbon Google’s strongest model yet. (Kavukcuoglu is leading Google DeepMind now that former CEO Demis Hassabis has stepped aside.) The post points to cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks, meaning complicated jobs that take many steps or run for a long time, as Carbon’s biggest strengths.
Each lab has claimed a new lead within weeks of the last.As with Argon, Google is announcing Carbon well before most people can use it.
22, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra earlier that month, and Google announced Argon on Sept.
Credit: Google The two benchmarks Carbon doesn’t win are worth noting.
Artificial Analysis runs a range of tests itself and combines them into a single composite score.On the newly updated version 5.0, Carbon (high) scores 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max).
All figures in this section are as reported by Google.
Carbon also makes about half as many unsupported claims as Argon.

Google is pitching Carbon on two things in particular: cybersecurity work and very long, complicated tasks.

So if you’re a small business already budgeting for Argon through the API, Google isn’t charging more for the new model, at least for now.

Think of it like a home inspector who has to find the crack in the foundation, decide whether it’s actually dangerous, and then patch it.

When Google calls Carbon “long-horizon,” it means the model is built to keep going through dead ends on a multi-step problem instead of quitting early. Picture a stubborn bug that takes a human engineer several days to fix. Google’s claim is that Carbon can keep working on that kind of bug for days at a time.

That’s an impressive claim. Keep in mind that it comes from Google’s own internal experience, not from an outside test. No independent lab has confirmed this ability outside of Google’s own reporting.

Google’s rollout plan explains a lot here. A model that’s good at finding and testing software weaknesses is useful to defenders, the people patching their own systems. We couldn’t independently confirm which figures belong to Argon versus Carbon in every secondary roundup. When comparing scores from unofficial sources, check carefully which model each number actually describes.

Google also shared a WebDev Arena result. Carbon gained 89 Elo points (a chess-style rating) to reach #4 at 1,768 . Google highlighted that as a big improvement, but it didn’t claim the top WebDev Arena spot.

This is the question everyone asks: is it better than ChatGPT or Claude? The short answer is that Carbon now tops one independent composite index, and there’s no head-to-head data yet for everyday tasks.

The one cross-vendor comparison from an independent tester is the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0, which rolls many evaluations into a single score. Google’s announcement says Carbon scores 59 there, and Artificial Analysis published an Oct. 28 article titled “Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5”:

We haven’t independently confirmed the current scores for Claude or ChatGPT models on that index, so we’ve left them out of the table rather than guess at the margin. Google’s headline security tests (SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym, CWE-bench) come from Google’s own announcement, so those scores are still Google’s own claims until outside testers reproduce them. Some non-official compilations, such as kie.ai , also circulate coding-test numbers for rival models, but none come from the model makers, so we’ve left them out.
Reaction to the official announcement is still forming, since it went out on Oct. 28.

Most of the online chatter so far predates the announcement. Before launch, Nokia Power User reported what it described as a Carbon checkpoint appearing on an AI arena; Google hasn’t confirmed that. Early tester write-ups, such as TestingCatalog’s , shared general impressions of unreleased builds without describing the builds, workloads, or conditions.
Those are anecdotes from unreleased test versions, not measured results, so don’t treat them as facts about the shipping model.

Who should wait: Pretty much everyone else. If you use Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude to draft emails, plan trips, or settle trivia arguments, nothing changes for you today. There’s no Carbon in your app and no release date. Also, Carbon’s best claimed skills, like finding exploits, aren’t things most of us do on a Tuesday afternoon.

Our view: the cautious rollout is the most interesting part of this announcement. Google is saying a model this good at security work shouldn’t be handed to everyone on day one. Artificial Analysis’s #1 listing is a good early sign, but Google’s security benchmark scores still need independent reproduction.
If you’re a regular user, your one practical step is to bookmark Google’s official announcement and check it for rollout updates instead of trusting release-date rumors.

Also, AI tools are getting better at finding software weaknesses, on both the defending and attacking sides. That makes basic security habits a little more important. Keep your devices updated, use a password manager , and consider a hardware security key for important accounts like email and banking. None of that needs Carbon, and all of it helps right now.

Gemini 4 Carbon is Google’s big claim that it has built a much stronger AI, especially for finding and fixing security holes and for sticking with hard problems for days. For now, it’s mostly available to security teams. Artificial Analysis now ranks it #1 on its Intelligence Index, but its headline security scores are still Google’s own figures. And there’s no date yet for when regular people can try it.
Honestly? That’s fine. A careful rollout for a security-focused model makes sense, and it gives outside testers time to check Google’s numbers before the hype takes over.

Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.
In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report .
With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.
Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment.
We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding.
With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena .

It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year. Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon . This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.

Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.

Gemini 4 Carbon reportedly makes big gains in cybersecurity applications. Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon. Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models. Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.

Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts. Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon. The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it. Its new model also beats GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1 in almost every test. Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests. extraction.body: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, a new frontier AI model that arrives just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon reached the Gemini app.In a blog post published Oct. 28, Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind, the company’s frontier AI lab, called Carbon Google’s strongest model yet. (Kavukcuoglu is leading Google DeepMind now that former CEO Demis Hassabis has stepped aside.) The post points to cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks, meaning complicated jobs that take many steps or run for a long time, as Carbon’s biggest strengths. Already, Gemini 4 Carbon has the top spot in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, beating out Claude Opus 5.5. Credit: Screenshot: Artificial Analysis SEE ALSO: Google says Gemini 4 Argon agents beat 'Minecraft' without human help The pace at which AI companies are releasing new frontier models has accelerated sharply in recent months, as the frontier AI labs race to have the best model available. 22, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra earlier that month, and Google announced Argon on Sept. 30 before releasing it to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers on Oct. Each lab has claimed a new lead within weeks of the last.As with Argon, Google is announcing Carbon well before most people can use it. Carbon is starting with a small group of cybersecurity defenders, and Google hasn’t said when it will reach everyone else. (Last week's PHP2Shell incident shows just how much havoc new AI models could wreak on the internet at large.) Announcing early lets Google claim the top spot on the leaderboards now. It also gives everyone a look at the benchmarks before the next round of releases.Gemini 4 Carbon: BenchmarksIn Google’s comparison table, Carbon posts the top score on 15 of 17 benchmarks against Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1. All figures in this section are as reported by Google. Credit: Google The two benchmarks Carbon doesn’t win are worth noting. Claude Opus 5.5 leads on OSWorld-2.1, which measures how well a model can operate a computer.A big change from Argon is that Google now reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 scores run by Artificial Analysis, an independent testing firm, rather than its own. For quick context, Terminal-Bench 4.0 measures how well an AI model can complete real technical tasks — like installing software or fixing broken code — by typing commands into a computer’s terminal on its own. It's one of the hardest agentic tests for LLMs.This is notable because the scores companies reported for each other’s models didn’t always line up with independent testing. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Carbon jumps about eight points over Argon and moves ahead of Opus 5.5.Google also says Carbon can work on difficult engineering problems for days at a time. Artificial Analysis runs a range of tests itself and combines them into a single composite score.On the newly updated version 5.0, Carbon (high) scores 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max). Gemini 4 Carbon's score of 59 is leaps above Argon's 50. Credit: Artificial Analysis The scores can’t be directly compared to the previous version of the index, where Argon (High) scored 53. A one-point lead is also thin enough that the next release from OpenAI or Anthropic could easily erase it. Carbon and Meta’s Muse Wonder Full are both flagged on the leaderboard as having no publicly available API, so they can’t yet be used outside their companies’ own access programs.Gemini 4 Carbon: Safety and safeguardsGoogle says Carbon uses the same safety system as Argon, which includes monitoring the model’s reasoning, and adds more work on alignment, or keeping the model behaving as intended. According to Google’s own testing, Carbon is also better behaved than its predecessor. Google says Carbon never successfully cheated on Terminal-Bench 4.0, meaning it never found a shortcut that passed a task without actually doing the work, and it tried to cheat only 0.4 percent of the time. During internal coding work, high-severity misalignment alerts, which flag a model acting in ways its developers didn’t intend, dropped by nearly 80 percent. Carbon also makes about half as many unsupported claims as Argon. And on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark, which tests whether hidden instructions can hijack a model, Carbon blocked every attack attempt, improving on Argon’s 0.7 percent attack success rate.All of these figures come from Google’s own testing.How to try Gemini 4 CarbonFor now, you can’t use Gemini 4 Carbon unless you’re an approved cyber defender in Google’s Fairwind Program. Starting this week, Carbon is rolling out to a small group of those testers, and Google says it will gradually add more trusted partners. Developers, businesses, and consumers will get access after that, but Google hasn’t given an exact public launch date.If we use Argon to figure out a timeline, about two weeks passed between its announcement and its arrival in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers. Though we won't be able to confirm whether Google will commit to that same schedule for Carbon.When Carbon does reach the API, Google says it will cost the same as Argon’s introductory price:$2 per million input tokens$10 per million output tokensCached input tokens at 95 percent off the input priceThat keeps Carbon well below its main rivals.

passages: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-context capabilities
Google is pitching Carbon on two things in particular: cybersecurity work and very long, complicated tasks.
The catch is that you almost certainly can’t use it today.
Starting this week, Google is giving it to a subset of cyber defenders (security teams), and it hasn’t said when regular people will get it.
The one cross-vendor comparison from an independent tester is the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0, which rolls many evaluations into a single score.
Google’s announcement says Carbon scores 59 there, and Artificial Analysis published an Oct.
For now, it’s mostly available to security teams.
Google says it builds on Gemini 4 Argon , which launched only about two weeks earlier.
That’s a fast turnaround, even by AI-industry standards.
If you just got used to the name “Argon,” we feel your pain.
So if you’re a small business already budgeting for Argon through the API, Google isn’t charging more for the new model, at least for now.
Google says that once the introductory period expires, Carbon will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, double the launch price.
Google also hasn’t announced any consumer pricing or a new subscription tier for Carbon, so don’t assume one exists.
Most of the online chatter so far predates the announcement.
Before launch, Nokia Power User reported what it described as a Carbon checkpoint appearing on an AI arena; Google hasn’t confirmed that.
Early tester write-ups, such as TestingCatalog’s , shared general impressions of unreleased builds without describing the builds, workloads, or conditions.
You ask, they answer, and if the problem is hard, they often stall or give you something half-finished.
When Google calls Carbon “long-horizon,” it means the model is built to keep going through dead ends on a multi-step problem instead of quitting early.
Picture a stubborn bug that takes a human engineer several days to fix.
Google’s claim is that Carbon can keep working on that kind of bug for days at a time.
For that last step, Google’s only wording is “as soon as possible.” That’s not a date.
There’s no confirmed timeline for when Carbon will appear in the regular Gemini app or any other consumer product.
Carbon gained 89 Elo points (a chess-style rating) to reach #4 at 1,768 .
Google highlighted that as a big improvement, but it didn’t claim the top WebDev Arena spot.
Here’s what Carbon is, why Google is leading with security, what it costs, and what’s still unproven (spoiler: quite a lot).
Google’s official announcement is the primary source for Google’s claims below; third-party sources are linked where we use them.
All sources were checked as of October 28, 2026.
It points to three security tests, and each one measures a different part of a security team’s job.
Think of it like a home inspector who has to find the crack in the foundation, decide whether it’s actually dangerous, and then patch it.
Google has published introductory API pricing .
An API is the way software developers plug an AI model into their own apps, so this is a price for businesses and developers, not a Gemini app subscription.
One email a week: new and updated guides from Online Tech Tips, plus the most-watched videos from our YouTube channel.
If you use Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude to draft emails, plan trips, or settle trivia arguments, nothing changes for you today.
Also, Carbon’s best claimed skills, like finding exploits, aren’t things most of us do on a Tuesday afternoon.
One thing to watch: benchmark numbers circulating online for tests like DeepSWE v1.1 and LVBench aren’t always clearly labeled by model version.
We couldn’t independently confirm which figures belong to Argon versus Carbon in every secondary roundup.

We haven’t independently confirmed the current scores for Claude or ChatGPT models on that index, so we’ve left them out of the table rather than guess at the margin.
Google’s headline security tests (SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym, CWE-bench) come from Google’s own announcement, so those scores are still Google’s own claims until outside testers reproduce them.
A model that’s good at finding and testing software weaknesses is useful to defenders, the people patching their own systems.
That same skill could also be useful to attackers.
Google describes this as responsible deployment.
In plain terms, it wants the good guys to get a head start.
Our view: the cautious rollout is the most interesting part of this announcement.
That makes basic security habits a little more important.
Keep your devices updated, use a password manager , and consider a hardware security key for important accounts like email and banking.
None of that needs Carbon, and all of it helps right now.

extraction.body: The Trump administration is giving Constellation Energy $5 billion in loans to expand nuclear generating capacity at eight power plants by 1.1 gigawatts. Most or all of the additional power from seven of those facilities has already been bought by Google, Meta, or Amazon. Constellation said it plans to use the financing to “uprate” 11 existing reactors, an industry term for expanding capacity at a reactor, often by using more highly enriched uranium and by upgrading equipment to handle the increased power levels. The energy company said it had already committed to spending more than $7 billion to add 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity to deliver power to Google, Amazon, and Meta. The loan commitment, which has yet to be finalized, “could lower financing costs” for the projects, Constellation said in a press release . The eight power plants include six in Illinois (Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, La Salle, and Quad Cities), one in Maryland (Calvert Cliffs), and one in Pennsylvania (Limerick). Google is already the confirmed buyer of additional power from the Pennsylvania plant and four Illinois power plants, while Amazon is buying electricity from the Maryland plant and Meta is effectively buying the entire Clinton power plant in Illinois. On Tuesday, the Department of Energy touted the loan as supporting “affordable, reliable power to American homes and businesses,” though there is no evidence that the new nuclear capacity will lower prices for residential ratepayers. Constellation’s announcement does not say whether the projects will maintain or lower electricity rates, and the company would not confirm the government’s claim to TechCrunch. Hyperscalers, including Google, Amazon, and Meta, have been scouring the grid for additional capacity to support their AI data centers. Tech companies are paying handsomely for energy, committing tens of billions of dollars over the coming years. Given that power has become a competitive advantage, that estimate is probably on the low end. By lowering the cost of capital for the upgrades, the Department of Energy’s loans could boost Constellation’s bottom line, that of the hyperscalers — or both. The energy company said it had already committed to spending more than $7 billion to add 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity to deliver power to Google, Amazon, and Meta. The loan commitment, which has yet to be finalized, “could lower financing costs” for the projects, Constellation said in a press release .
The eight power plants include six in Illinois (Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, La Salle, and Quad Cities), one in Maryland (Calvert Cliffs), and one in Pennsylvania (Limerick).

Google is already the confirmed buyer of additional power from the Pennsylvania plant and four Illinois power plants, while Amazon is buying electricity from the Maryland plant and Meta is effectively buying the entire Clinton power plant in Illinois.

On Tuesday, the Department of Energy touted the loan as supporting “affordable, reliable power to American homes and businesses,” though there is no evidence that the new nuclear capacity will lower prices for residential ratepayers. Constellation’s announcement does not say whether the projects will maintain or lower electricity rates, and the company would not confirm the government’s claim to TechCrunch.

Hyperscalers, including Google, Amazon, and Meta, have been scouring the grid for additional capacity to support their AI data centers. Tech companies are paying handsomely for energy, committing tens of billions of dollars over the coming years. Given that power has become a competitive advantage, that estimate is probably on the low end.
By lowering the cost of capital for the upgrades, the Department of Energy’s loans could boost Constellation’s bottom line, that of the hyperscalers — or both.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor.

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. sources.title: Apple's Redesigned MacBook Pro Has An OLED Touchscreen, Weighs Just Three Pounds - Engadget
passages: The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, as it's officially called, is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, just like the non-touch models.
And as a nice throwback to older Apple laptops, its rear Apple logo also lights up.
As part of the new design, the OLED MacBook Pro features a Dynamic Island around its webcam, and Apple claims the 14-inch model weighs just three pounds.
That's a noticeable difference from the current MacBook Pro, which clocks in at 3.4 pounds.
Apple finally announced its long-rumored redesign today, and for the most part, it seems like the company went out of its way to create its most premium laptop yet.
It's clearly not meant for a regular consumer.
And thankfully, you've still got a useful array of ports: three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C connections, MagSafe, HDMI, headphone jack and an SDXC card slot.

It makes the simple act of casually scrolling through articles and content easier, as we've seen on touchscreen-equipped Windows PC over the last 15 years.
But in the demo video above, we can also see people swiping on media and manipulating 3D objects.
It also looks like you can interact with iOS apps just as they would with a phone, which would be particularly useful to developers.

I can only imagine the eye-searing possibilities with this screen.
It also features a 120Hz refresh rate, just like existing MacBook Pros.
Thanks to the slimmer bezels, Apple was also able to squeeze in larger 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens.

There's no doubt Apple is late here, but there was also a certain wisdom in completely separating its touchscreen platforms (iOS, iPadOS and watchOS) from macOS, a platform that was designed entirely around traditional computer inputs.
With Windows 8, Microsoft rushed to enable PC touchscreens as a way to compete with the potential rise of iPads.
Apple didn't have the same pressure — especially since its glass touchpads offer an incredibly smooth scrolling experience on Macs.
