extraction.body: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro has arrived with a price tag that pushes the company’s premium laptop strategy to a new extreme. While the new 14-inch model starts at $2,899 in the US, selecting the highest-end components for the 16-inch version can raise the total to $14,549. The figures, reported by TechCrunch following Apple’s launch on 28 October, highlight how expensive the new MacBook Pro range can become once buyers move beyond the standard configurations. The fully upgraded 14-inch model reaches $14,249, according to Apple’s online configurator pricing cited in the report. Storage is one of the biggest contributors to the final bill. According to TechCrunch, upgrading to a 4TB SSD adds $1,000, while the 8TB option costs an additional $3,000. Choosing the new 16TB maximum adds $7,000 to the configuration. The memory upgrade is similarly costly. Moving to 128GB of unified memory adds $2,000, while nano-texture glass carries a further $150 charge. These upgrades are aimed at demanding professional workloads, including video production, 3D work and other tasks involving large files or memory-intensive applications. However, their combined cost means buyers need to assess carefully whether they will use the additional capacity enough to justify the expense. The new 16-inch model’s $14,549 maximum is $4,400 higher than the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro’s reported top configuration of $10,149. That is a substantial increase for a product category that was already positioned at the premium end of the laptop market. The price increase accompanies a major change to the MacBook Pro’s display and interaction model. Apple’s new 14-inch and 16-inch machines introduce touchscreen support to the Mac for the first time, paired with a tandem OLED display marketed as PROLED XDR. Apple says the screen supports a 120Hz variable refresh rate, up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The display also supports both P3 and Adobe RGB colour spaces, features intended to appeal to photographers, designers and video professionals. The laptops use Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, offer up to 128GB of unified memory and support storage configurations of up to 16TB. Apple also says the redesigned machines deliver up to 24 hours of battery life and feature a thinner, lighter enclosure. Touch input is designed to complement rather than replace the keyboard and trackpad. Users can interact directly with content, manipulate creative projects and use touch-enabled controls in compatible applications. A redesigned hinge is intended to keep the display stable when users tap or swipe across it. The new models also bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, providing access to features including Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. The launch is a notable departure for Apple, whose executives previously resisted touchscreen laptops. But the pricing raises a practical question: how many customers will pay the premium for direct screen interaction and the new display? Reuters reported that PC makers shipped 33.4 million touchscreen notebooks in 2025, with an average selling price of about $1,009. That figure is far below even Apple’s entry-level touchscreen MacBook Pro price, placing the new machines in a much narrower market aimed at professionals and affluent enthusiasts. Apple’s US starting prices are $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch M5Pro model. Higher-end M5 Max versions start at $4,499 and $4,799, respectively. Pre-orders opened on 28 October, with retail availability scheduled to begin on 6 November. For most buyers, the maximum configuration is unlikely to make financial sense unless their work genuinely demands that much memory and storage. The headline price nevertheless demonstrates how far Apple is willing to take its premium positioning as it adds touchscreen functionality to its professional laptop range. The bottom line: Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro combines a major display upgrade with new ways to interact with macOS, but optional memory and storage upgrades can push the 16-inch model to $14,549. For professionals who need the maximum configuration, that may be a workable business expense; for everyone else, the starting price is already a substantial commitment. Apple says the screen supports a 120Hz variable refresh rate, up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The display also supports both P3 and Adobe RGB colour spaces, features intended to appeal to photographers, designers and video professionals.

The laptops use Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, offer up to 128GB of unified memory and support storage configurations of up to 16TB. Apple also says the redesigned machines deliver up to 24 hours of battery life and feature a thinner, lighter enclosure.

Touch input is designed to complement rather than replace the keyboard and trackpad. Users can interact directly with content, manipulate creative projects and use touch-enabled controls in compatible applications. A redesigned hinge is intended to keep the display stable when users tap or swipe across it.
The new models also bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, providing access to features including Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI.

The launch is a notable departure for Apple, whose executives previously resisted touchscreen laptops. But the pricing raises a practical question: how many customers will pay the premium for direct screen interaction and the new display?

Reuters reported that PC makers shipped 33.4 million touchscreen notebooks in 2025, with an average selling price of about $1,009. That figure is far below even Apple’s entry-level touchscreen MacBook Pro price, placing the new machines in a much narrower market aimed at professionals and affluent enthusiasts.

Apple’s US starting prices are $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch M5Pro model. Higher-end M5 Max versions start at $4,499 and $4,799, respectively. Pre-orders opened on 28 October, with retail availability scheduled to begin on 6 November.

For most buyers, the maximum configuration is unlikely to make financial sense unless their work genuinely demands that much memory and storage. The headline price nevertheless demonstrates how far Apple is willing to take its premium positioning as it adds touchscreen functionality to its professional laptop range.

The bottom line: Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro combines a major display upgrade with new ways to interact with macOS, but optional memory and storage upgrades can push the 16-inch model to $14,549. For professionals who need the maximum configuration, that may be a workable business expense; for everyone else, the starting price is already a substantial commitment.

coreStoryFacts.text: The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, as it's officially called, is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, just like the non-touch models.
And as a nice throwback to older Apple laptops, its rear Apple logo also lights up.
As part of the new design, the OLED MacBook Pro features a Dynamic Island around its webcam, and Apple claims the 14-inch model weighs just three pounds.
That's a noticeable difference from the current MacBook Pro, which clocks in at 3.4 pounds.
Apple finally announced its long-rumored redesign today, and for the most part, it seems like the company went out of its way to create its most premium laptop yet.
It's clearly not meant for a regular consumer.
And thankfully, you've still got a useful array of ports: three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C connections, MagSafe, HDMI, headphone jack and an SDXC card slot.
So what's the point of a touchscreen MacBook Pro?
It makes the simple act of casually scrolling through articles and content easier, as we've seen on touchscreen-equipped Windows PC over the last 15 years.
But in the demo video above, we can also see people swiping on media and manipulating 3D objects.
It also looks like you can interact with iOS apps just as they would with a phone, which would be particularly useful to developers.
Third-party creator apps like Notion, Canva, Powerpoint and Blender will also work with the touchscreen natively.
The ProLED XDR screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, according to Apple, and it features an "industry-leading" 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
I can only imagine the eye-searing possibilities with this screen.
It also features a 120Hz refresh rate, just like existing MacBook Pros.
Thanks to the slimmer bezels, Apple was also able to squeeze in larger 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens.

Apple didn't have the same pressure — especially since its glass touchpads offer an incredibly smooth scrolling experience on Macs.
Absurd prices aside, the launch marks a significant shift for Apple, nearly a decade after it first experimented with the Touch Bar .
The company eventually abandoned that feature, but now it’s ready to embrace a touchscreen MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro has arrived with a price tag that pushes the company’s premium laptop strategy to a new extreme. While the new 14-inch model starts at $2,899 in the US, selecting the highest-end components for the 16-inch version can raise the total to $14,549. The figures, reported by TechCrunch following Apple’s launch on 28 October, highlight how expensive the new MacBook Pro range can become once buyers move beyond the standard configurations. The fully upgraded 14-inch model reaches $14,249, according to Apple’s online configurator pricing cited in the report. Storage is one of the biggest contributors to the final bill. According to TechCrunch, upgrading to a 4TB SSD adds $1,000, while the 8TB option costs an additional $3,000. Choosing the new 16TB maximum adds $7,000 to the configuration. The memory upgrade is similarly costly. Moving to 128GB of unified memory adds $2,000, while nano-texture glass carries a further $150 charge. These upgrades are aimed at demanding professional workloads, including video production, 3D work and other tasks involving large files or memory-intensive applications. However, their combined cost means buyers need to assess carefully whether they will use the additional capacity enough to justify the expense. The new 16-inch model’s $14,549 maximum is $4,400 higher than the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro’s reported top configuration of $10,149. That is a substantial increase for a product category that was already positioned at the premium end of the laptop market. The price increase accompanies a major change to the MacBook Pro’s display and interaction model. Apple’s new 14-inch and 16-inch machines introduce touchscreen support to the Mac for the first time, paired with a tandem OLED display marketed as PROLED XDR. Apple says the screen supports a 120Hz variable refresh rate, up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The display also supports both P3 and Adobe RGB colour spaces, features intended to appeal to photographers, designers and video professionals. The laptops use Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, offer up to 128GB of unified memory and support storage configurations of up to 16TB. Apple also says the redesigned machines deliver up to 24 hours of battery life and feature a thinner, lighter enclosure. Touch input is designed to complement rather than replace the keyboard and trackpad. Users can interact directly with content, manipulate creative projects and use touch-enabled controls in compatible applications. A redesigned hinge is intended to keep the display stable when users tap or swipe across it. The new models also bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, providing access to features including Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. The launch is a notable departure for Apple, whose executives previously resisted touchscreen laptops. But the pricing raises a practical question: how many customers will pay the premium for direct screen interaction and the new display? Reuters reported that PC makers shipped 33.4 million touchscreen notebooks in 2025, with an average selling price of about $1,009. That figure is far below even Apple’s entry-level touchscreen MacBook Pro price, placing the new machines in a much narrower market aimed at professionals and affluent enthusiasts. Apple’s US starting prices are $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro model and $3,399 for the 16-inch M5Pro model. Higher-end M5 Max versions start at $4,499 and $4,799, respectively. Pre-orders opened on 28 October, with retail availability scheduled to begin on 6 November. For most buyers, the maximum configuration is unlikely to make financial sense unless their work genuinely demands that much memory and storage. The headline price nevertheless demonstrates how far Apple is willing to take its premium positioning as it adds touchscreen functionality to its professional laptop range. The bottom line: Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro combines a major display upgrade with new ways to interact with macOS, but optional memory and storage upgrades can push the 16-inch model to $14,549. For professionals who need the maximum configuration, that may be a workable business expense; for everyone else, the starting price is already a substantial commitment. extraction.body: Apple on Tuesday unveiled its new 14-inch MacBook Pro, powered by its latest M6 chip. The new MacBook Pro has 24 hours of battery life and now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity. The laptop starts at $1,999 and is available in space black and silver. Apple also announced its latest iMac , which is also powered by the M6 chip. The tech giant revealed the new devices just a day before its “Pro and Tell” event scheduled for Wednesday. On Monday, Apple announced its new iPad mini . The tech giant says the M6 chip features a 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that delivers more responsive performance, up to 30% faster graphics, and up to 25% faster AI workloads compared with the M5 chip. The M6 delivers up to 13 times the LLM prompt-processing speed of the M1 MacBook Pro and up to 1.3 times faster performance than the M5 model, Apple says. The M6 MacBook Pro starts with 16GB of unified memory, configurable up to 32GB, and has memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s, up from the 153GB/s on the M5 chip. It includes HDMI, MagSafe 3, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an SDXC card slot, and a headphone jack. Like previous models, the laptop features a 12-megapixel camera. The M6 MacBook Pro supports fast charging, reaching up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with a compatible high-wattage USB-C power adapter. As for the new M6-powered iMac, it features a faster CPU and GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every core. Apple says the M6 delivers smooth multitasking and powerful performance for everyday apps, photo editing, and video production. The new iMac starts at $1,499 and comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver. The company also notes that the new iMac delivers up to five times faster on-device AI performance than the M4 model. The laptop supports fast charging, allowing it to reach up to 50 percent battery capacity in 30 minutes when paired with a compatible higher-wattage USB-C power adapter, such as Apple’s 96W adapter.
The new MacBook Pro retains its 14-inch Liquid Retina XDR display, which offers up to 1,600 nits of peak HDR brightness and a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
Apple also offers an optional nano-texture display finish designed to reduce reflections and glare in challenging lighting conditions.
Apple says the new MacBook Pro is manufactured using renewable electricity across its supply chain and is designed to be durable and repairable.

Apple says the new MacBook Pro will be available soon through the Philippine Apple Store online and Apple Authorized Resellers. Local availability details have yet to be announced.
For years, users have been asking Apple to make the iPad run some hybrid of iPadOS and macOS.

The MacBook Neo and iPad Pro are proof that this isn’t too farfetched. The former runs macOS on an iPhone/iPad chip (A-series) while the latter runs iPadOS on a MacBook chip (M-series). Computing power doesn’t seem to be the issue. Apple is just likely afraid that one device category will cannibalize the other. That’s pure speculation on my part so let’s just continue with the thought exercise.
Assuming we get that macOS and iPadOS hybrid, what will the hardware look like?
Apple has unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, introducing tandem OLED technology and touchscreen capabilities to the Mac for the first time.

Available in 14-inch and 16-inch models, the new MacBook Pro combines a redesigned display with Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. It also introduces the Dynamic Island to Mac, alongside improvements to graphics performance, on-device AI, and battery life.

Apple says the new MacBook Pro delivers up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR and SDR brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and a 120Hz variable refresh rate. The laptop also offers up to 24 hours of battery life in a thinner and lighter design.
The new MacBook Pro introduces Apple’s PROLED XDR display, which uses tandem OLED technology to improve brightness, contrast, and color accuracy.

Unlike conventional OLED designs, the display uses two self-illuminating pixel layers. Apple says this approach helps maintain brightness and grayscale uniformity while minimizing internal reflections.

extraction.body: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage. It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers. The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too. The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port. There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6. sources.title: Apple's M6 chip brings serious on-device AI power to the entry-level MacBook Pro and the colorful iMac - XDA
passages: Ahead of its upcoming "Pro and Tell" event, Apple has revealed its refreshed 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac , powered by its M6 chip.
This means the new MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, a full HDMI port, and an SD card slot.
While this isn't exactly surprising, given Apple's MacBook Pro design has been around for several years now, it would have been nice to see it evolve in some way.
Apple also refreshed its all-in-one iMac with the M6 chip .
This update comes two years after the colorful computer got the M4 chip (the iMac skipped the M5 series entirely).
The base M6 configuration in the iMac features a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, a step up from the 8-core M4 CPU in the last-generation iMac.

Apple says that the M6 features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, emphasizing that it's a powerful platform for local LLMs and that the chip is designed to take full advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.
The MacBook M6 also features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, alongside returning features like the 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and Liquid Retina XDR display with optional nano-texture.
The entry-level iMac starts at $1,500 and will be available to pre-order on October 28th, with shipping starting on November 6th.
Apple also recently revealed its A20-powered iPad mini .
At its upcoming event, the tech giant is expected to show off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook for the first time.

Interestingly, the company also compares the M6 to the M1 in its press release, highlighting that the newer, more powerful chip offers 11x faster graphics and up to 13x faster AI performance. Apple says that the M6 features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, emphasizing that it's a powerful platform for local LLMs and that the chip is designed to take full advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. Beyond the bump up to the M6 chip, the entry-level 14-inch MacBook features the same overall design and port layout as last year's M5 upgrade and, in fact, the year prior's M4 refresh. This means the new MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, a full HDMI port, and an SD card slot. While this isn't exactly surprising, given Apple's MacBook Pro design has been around for several years now, it would have been nice to see it evolve in some way. Pricing for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro starts at $2,000 for the 16GB version, which matches last year's pricing. Pre-orders start on October 28th, with shipping beginning on November 6th. Apple also refreshed its all-in-one iMac with the M6 chip . This update comes two years after the colorful computer got the M4 chip (the iMac skipped the M5 series entirely). The base M6 configuration in the iMac features a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, a step up from the 8-core M4 CPU in the last-generation iMac. There's also a more expensive 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU configuration Beyond the chip upgrade, there isn't much else new. The refreshed iMac features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 like the new 14-inch MacBook Pro. It also has the same Thunderbolt ports as the M4 iMac — two on the 10-core and four on the 12-core. The colors are all the same too: Blue, Purple, Pink, Orange, Yellow, Green, and Silver. At the very least, it would have been great to see an iMac color refresh and a port selection that made a bit more sense. The entry-level iMac starts at $1,500 and will be available to pre-order on October 28th, with shipping starting on November 6th. The M6 MacBook Pro and iMac follow the M6 Mac Mini that Apple revealed earlier this year, which the company somewhat confusingly showed off alongside the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. The M6 is Apple's first 2nm chip and bumps up to a 12-core CPU from the M5's 10 cores. Apple also recently revealed its A20-powered iPad mini . At its upcoming event, the tech giant is expected to show off its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook for the first time. The redesigned tablet also features a thinner and lighter design. I love my MacBook Pro M5 and hope it lasts me as long as my M1 did. What confuses me is why so much emphasis is put on the device's bigger, better performance, but most people are running most things online now, so the performance is surely about the weakest link... Usually the speed of the internet and connection at the time you are using it. Nobody really focuses on that. I'm sure my Antigravity work sessions would be improved greatly by a much better and consistent internet connection than a slightly faster processor in my Mac. Just food for thought.

Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line. The new iMac and MacBook Pro, unveiled on Oct 27 , are visually similar to their predecessors – with the main changes happening internally. Both machines now include the M6 chip, which debuted in the Mac mini in September. The iMac is moving from an M4 processor, while the MacBook Pro received the M5 in 2025 . The updates represent a second day of Apple announcements this week, with the company rolling out a revamped iPad mini on Oct 26 with a new screen and water resistance. Apple will cap the launches on Oct 28 with its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Bloomberg News has reported. The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-orders on Oct 28 and will arrive beginning Nov 6, Apple said, matching the new iPad mini. The new iMac starts at US$1,499 (S$1,920), while the MacBook Pro begins at US$1,999. Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics. The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines. The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac also include Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7, while the laptop gets faster charging. Both machines go on sale Nov. 6 after pre-orders open on Oct 28 . The new Macs come as part of a slew of changes to the company’s computer line. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 . The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028. Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

The new iMac and MacBook Pro, unveiled on Oct 27 , are visually similar to their predecessors – with the main changes happening internally. Both machines now include the M6 chip, which debuted in the Mac mini in September. The iMac is moving from an M4 processor, while the MacBook Pro received the M5 in 2025 .

The updates represent a second day of Apple announcements this week, with the company rolling out a revamped iPad mini on Oct 26 with a new screen and water resistance. Apple will cap the launches on Oct 28 with its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Bloomberg News has reported.

The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-orders on Oct 28 and will arrive beginning Nov 6, Apple said, matching the new iPad mini. The new iMac starts at US$1,499 (S$1,920), while the MacBook Pro begins at US$1,999.
Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics.
The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines.
The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac also include Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7, while the laptop gets faster charging. Both machines go on sale Nov. 6 after pre-orders open on Oct 28 .

The new Macs come as part of a slew of changes to the company’s computer line. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 .
The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028.
Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

extraction.body: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM but can go to 4TB of storage. It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers. The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too. The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance. In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port. There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. Preorders start October 28, and they ship November 6. Apple has rolled out a new 24-inch iMac and an entry-level MacBook Pro with a 14-inch screen, marking key updates in an end-to-end overhaul of the company’s computer line. The new iMac and MacBook Pro, unveiled on Oct 27 , are visually similar to their predecessors – with the main changes happening internally. Both machines now include the M6 chip, which debuted in the Mac mini in September. The iMac is moving from an M4 processor, while the MacBook Pro received the M5 in 2025 . The updates represent a second day of Apple announcements this week, with the company rolling out a revamped iPad mini on Oct 26 with a new screen and water resistance. Apple will cap the launches on Oct 28 with its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Bloomberg News has reported. The updated iMac and low-end MacBook Pro become available for pre-orders on Oct 28 and will arrive beginning Nov 6, Apple said, matching the new iPad mini. The new iMac starts at US$1,499 (S$1,920), while the MacBook Pro begins at US$1,999. Apple said the M6 chip makes the iMac five times faster than the prior model from 2024 for artificial intelligence, while the new MacBook Pro is 30% speedier than its predecessor for graphics. The company continues to sell higher-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, which have more advanced main processing and graphics cores compared with the entry M6 machines. The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac also include Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7, while the laptop gets faster charging. Both machines go on sale Nov. 6 after pre-orders open on Oct 28 . The new Macs come as part of a slew of changes to the company’s computer line. Beyond the push into touchscreen displays, Apple is preparing a refreshed MacBook Neo and MacBook Air for the first half of 2027 . The company is also working on a redesigned low-end MacBook Pro and the release of its first M7, M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in 2027. It is planning an M7 Ultra and a new Mac Studio in 2028. Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro with a touchscreen – coming on Oct 28 – will include a lighter and slightly thinner design, slimmer bezels around the display and OLED technology, Bloomberg reported.

sources.title: Hands-on with Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro
passages: The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models.
Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps.
Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one.
Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface.
That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line.
And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen.
While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly.

Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app.
On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook.

extraction.body: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side by side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup, which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best and infuriating at worst. Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is. On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: It’s not as different from the previous model as you might have expected. LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference. The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout. And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic. Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea. I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen. A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop: All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more. When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro. It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality. I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature. Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that. Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows. I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro.
It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality.

I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature.

Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that.
Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows.

I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

passages: However, the upcoming Pro model could be thinner and considerably lighter than current models while also adding support for a touchscreen.In the latest edition of the Power On newsletter, Bloomberg s Mark Gurman claimed that the next-generation MacBook Pro models will have several design changes with a re-engineered internal layout that includes miniaturised and rearranged components to reduce the overall weight of the device.The current 16-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Max chip weighs around 2.15 kg, whereas the 15-inch MacBook Air weighs only about 1.5 kg.

Several other reports in the past have also pointed towards this feature alongside a Dynamic Island-style cutout or interface element for Apple s laptop.This comes at the same time as the new CEO, John Ternus, is said to have taken a significant interest in both of Apple s design teams across industrial design and human interface.
Alongside a slimmer and lighter body, the redesigned laptop is also tipped to feature a touchscreen OLED panel, which will be a first for the MacBook.

extraction.body: Steve Jobs famously called touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible,” and for over a decade, Apple stridently refused to make one. Today that all changes with the MacBook Pro — the company’s first laptop to embrace a touch interface. While it’s unlikely that Apple can fix all the “terrible” ergonomics of having to lift your arm up and touch a laptop screen, the company has put some effort into making macOS more touch-friendly. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display weighs just 3 pounds, which is noticeably lighter than the current generation of non-touch MacBook Pros, which start at 3.4 pounds for the newly introduced M6 models. The difference is even bigger when you jump to the 16-inch model, which clocks in at 4 pounds, while the M5 Pro version without a touchscreen is 4.7. It still has heft, but it feels better balanced when picking it up from a corner with one hand. Putting it side by side with a current 16-inch MacBook Pro, you see that it’s slightly thinner and has a footprint a smidge smaller. It’s a seemingly minor feature, but one that definitely got the audience excited during the introduction, and marks the return of a bit of flair to the MacBook lineup, which, let’s be fair, has grown a bit utilitarian-looking over the years. Touch works almost exactly like you’d expect it to with Apple’s first-party apps. That said, anyone who has tried to “click” a tiny button in an app with their finger knows it’s a pretty fiddly experience at best and infuriating at worst. Apple is trying to address this, at least slightly, by magnifying some controls when you poke at them — like the red, yellow, and green traffic light buttons in the top left corner of windows to close, minimize, and maximize an app. And while MacBook Pro hinges are pretty solid, yes, you can make it wobble pretty easily with some firm taps toward the top of the screen. The OLED is punchy, bright, contrasty, and saturated. Without more time to do side-by-side comparisons, it’s hard to tell just how much of an improvement the OLED XDR display is. On first impression, at least, the touchscreen doesn’t seem likely to revolutionize the MacBook. That’s why it’s just a MacBook Pro variant and not an entirely new product line. Unsurprisingly, there is a price premium for the new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. The touchscreen OLED model starts at $2,899, $400 more than the otherwise similarly-specced M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: It’s not as different from the previous model as you might have expected. LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference. The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout. And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic. Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea. I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen. A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop: All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more. When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images. But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro. It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality. I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature. Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that. Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows. I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. passages: Michael Saylor, founder and executive chairman of Strategy ( MSTR ), the world's largest public holder of bitcoin, said in an interview during Yahoo Finance's Invest event , "There's no doubt in my mind, bitcoin will be a larger asset class than gold by the year 2035."
When asked about the swoon in Strategy's stock over the past month and whether bitcoin believers are losing steam, Saylor pushed back, saying, "I don't think they're losing faith."

Saylor's bullish outlook comes after prices for bitcoin, smaller digital assets, and crypto-linked stocks such as Strategy have seen a fierce correction since mid-October, with billions of dollars in leveraged positions within the crypto derivatives market unwinding in recent weeks, according to data tracked by aggregator CoinGlass.
Though it also has underperformed against the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ), bitcoin has still risen 9%.

Strategy, once a business intelligence software company known as MicroStrategy, has transformed under Saylor into an investment vehicle that churns out a hypervolatile bitcoin equity offering and a range of bond instruments.
Based on that production schedule, by 2035, 99% of all the bitcoin will have been created, Saylor noted.
Bitcoin currently has a market cap of approximately $2.04 trillion, versus gold's $29.2 trillion.
For bitcoin to surpass gold, its price would need to climb above $1.4 million per coin.
Long seen as digital gold, the comparison between bitcoin's and gold ( GC=F ) this year appears to indicate that investors for now prefer gold to its digital variation.
Gold has outperformed bitcoin by 52% since the beginning of the year.

extraction.body: Bitcoin has a current market cap of $1.6 trillion, compared to $28 trillion for physical gold. If Bitcoin grows at its historical annual rate of 37%, it could surpass gold in market cap within the next decade. Stablecoins, which are growing at an exponential rate, pose a potential threat to Bitcoin. Although Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is sometimes referred to as digital gold, it still has quite a way to go before it catches up to physical gold in market value. At a current market cap of $1.6 trillion, Bitcoin is only one-seventeenth the size of gold, which has a market cap of $28 trillion. However, if Bitcoin can continue growing at its historical rate of 37% per year, it could surpass gold within the next decade. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Bitcoin's lifetime supply is fixed at a hard cap of 21 million coins. Already, slightly more than 20 million of these coins are in circulation, so we are getting very close to the point where all the Bitcoin that will ever exist already does. This introduces increasing scarcity and is the primary reason Bitcoin has earned the moniker digital gold. Best of all, the rate of new Bitcoin supply (for the remaining 1 million coins not in circulation) is carefully controlled by an algorithm. There is no central bank, sovereign government, or financial institution that can change it. This prevents the value of Bitcoin from being inflated away by increasing the supply. Over time, Bitcoin is actually disinflationary, because every four years, the rate of new Bitcoin creation is cut in half (via the Bitcoin halving mechanism). This is why a growing number of investors now turn to Bitcoin as a potential store of value and a hedge against inflation. Even former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell agrees. Back in December 2024, he called Bitcoin a modern form of gold: "It's like gold -- it's just virtual and digital." That said, the digital gold argument goes in and out of favor every few years. Right now, it's making a comeback amid growing concerns about U.S. fiscal irresponsibility. A $40 trillion national debt load will almost certainly lead to higher inflation, the thinking goes, if the Fed is forced to print more money to pay it off. For that reason, crypto investors have repeatedly made the case for Bitcoin as the ultimate form of sound money, and a potential alternative to fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar. To surpass physical gold in market cap, though, Bitcoin will need to become less volatile. It's hard to make the argument for Bitcoin as digital gold or as a form of sound money when its value fluctuates so much on a daily, weekly, monthly, and annual basis. This volatility is the primary reason Bitcoin has never fulfilled its initial promise to become a medium of exchange. Imagine going on vacation to a foreign country, where the exchange rate zigzags wildly on a daily basis. You might think twice about making a purchase in that country, especially if you are on a tight budget. For that reason, stablecoins have been eating Bitcoin's lunch recently. They have grown exponentially in size and are now a $300 billion industry. Stablecoins, as their name would suggest, are stable in value. Most are pegged to the U.S. dollar on a 1:1 basis, making them extraordinarily useful as a medium of exchange. As a result, some top investors have scaled back their future price targets for Bitcoin to account for the growing role of stablecoins. For example, Cathie Wood of Ark Invest has cut her 2030 Bitcoin price target from $1.5 million to $1.2 million. According to Wood, dollar-pegged stablecoins are scaling much faster than anticipated and capturing transactional volume in markets that Ark Invest previously expected Bitcoin to dominate. But guess what? A price of $1.2 million still works. That price implies a $25 trillion market cap for Bitcoin by the year 2030. Saylor's bullish outlook comes after prices for bitcoin, smaller digital assets, and crypto-linked stocks such as Strategy have seen a fierce correction since mid-October, with billions of dollars in leveraged positions within the crypto derivatives market unwinding in recent weeks, according to data tracked by aggregator CoinGlass.
Though it also has underperformed against the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ), bitcoin has still risen 9%.

passages: Although Bitcoin ( BTC -1.43% ) is sometimes referred to as digital gold, it still has quite a way to go before it catches up to physical gold in market value. At a current market cap of $1.6 trillion, Bitcoin is only one-seventeenth the size of gold, which has a market cap of $28 trillion.
However, if Bitcoin can continue growing at its historical rate of 37% per year, it could surpass gold within the next decade.

Bitcoin's lifetime supply is fixed at a hard cap of 21 million coins. Already, slightly more than 20 million of these coins are in circulation, so we are getting very close to the point where all the Bitcoin that will ever exist already does. This introduces increasing scarcity and is the primary reason Bitcoin has earned the moniker digital gold.

Best of all, the rate of new Bitcoin supply (for the remaining 1 million coins not in circulation) is carefully controlled by an algorithm. There is no central bank, sovereign government, or financial institution that can change it. This prevents the value of Bitcoin from being inflated away by increasing the supply. Over time, Bitcoin is actually disinflationary, because every four years, the rate of new Bitcoin creation is cut in half (via the Bitcoin halving mechanism).

This is why a growing number of investors now turn to Bitcoin as a potential store of value and a hedge against inflation. Even former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell agrees. Back in December 2024, he called Bitcoin a modern form of gold: "It's like gold -- it's just virtual and digital."

That said, the digital gold argument goes in and out of favor every few years. Right now, it's making a comeback amid growing concerns about U.S. fiscal irresponsibility. A $40 trillion national debt load will almost certainly lead to higher inflation, the thinking goes, if the Fed is forced to print more money to pay it off.
For that reason, crypto investors have repeatedly made the case for Bitcoin as the ultimate form of sound money, and a potential alternative to fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar.

To surpass physical gold in market cap, though, Bitcoin will need to become less volatile. It's hard to make the argument for Bitcoin as digital gold or as a form of sound money when its value fluctuates so much on a daily, weekly, monthly, and annual basis.

This volatility is the primary reason Bitcoin has never fulfilled its initial promise to become a medium of exchange. Imagine going on vacation to a foreign country, where the exchange rate zigzags wildly on a daily basis. You might think twice about making a purchase in that country, especially if you are on a tight budget.

For that reason, stablecoins have been eating Bitcoin's lunch recently. They have grown exponentially in size and are now a $300 billion industry. Stablecoins, as their name would suggest, are stable in value. Most are pegged to the U.S. dollar on a 1:1 basis, making them extraordinarily useful as a medium of exchange.

As a result, some top investors have scaled back their future price targets for Bitcoin to account for the growing role of stablecoins. extraction.body: Every week, the company has been introducing new devices and products. So here's a nifty roundup. Rather than hold a standard fall hardware event, Amazon has been announcing new products piecemeal over the last several weeks. It's a savvy move on the company's part to help keep its devices in consumers' minds instead of revealing a ton of stuff all at once that people may quickly forget about. Remember that microwave it once made? It seems the company's chief of Alexa and devices Panos Panay might agree. He recently told Engadget that "last year was a fine moment, but it turns out only two products really got any attention and everything else was just there." He also felt that the teams behind the overlooked products didn't get to take the pride that they, he felt, deserved. Well, we're here to help you keep up with all the things the company has announced in recent weeks. For a start, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of tablets that actually won't force you to resort to a workaround to access the Google Play Store . The latest batch of Kindles is here too, along with fresh Ring smart home gear and an updated Fire TV Stick 4K. Bee, a maker of AI note-taking devices, showed off its first new products since joining Amazon last year. Amazon has also teased that there are more Alexa-branded devices on the way . Here's a breakdown of the new devices Amazon announced so far in October. Amazon is transitioning away from Fire tablets to a new, more premium lineup of devices. Alexa tablets are now available in the US, Mexico, Canada, UK, Germany, France, Italy and Spain. They come in three sizes, the two smallest of which are primarily for entertainment purposes. The Alexa Tablet 8 (which starts at $230) has a 8.7-inch display, an 8-core CPU, 2-core GPU, 4GB of RAM and 64GB or 128GB of storage. It's 0.3 inches thick and weighs 16.4 ounces, so it's the most portable of the bunch. Amazon says it offers up to 14 hours of video playback and 19 hours of Kindle reading (more on that shortly) on a charge. Next up, we have the Alexa Tablet 11, which boasts a 2.5K, 11-inch display with a 90Hz refresh rate and a 16:10 cinematic aspect ratio. Along with an 8-core CPU and 2-core CPU, it has a fifth-gen MDLA NPU to support on-device AI processing. The tablet also has 8GB of RAM, the same storage options as its smaller sibling and dual Dolby Atmos speakers. The battery will deliver up to 15 hours of video playback, Amazon claims. This tablet starts at $330. Then there's the flagship model, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which costs $500. Amazon says it's the most powerful model yet, with "three times faster processing and nine times faster graphics" than any of its previous tablets. The 12-inch, 280 PPI display has a 120Hz refresh rate and a 3:2 aspect ratio. The tablet has an 8-core CPU, 7-core GPU, 8th-gen MDLA NPU, 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. Battery life tops out at 16 hours for video playback and 20 hours for Kindle usage, Amazon says. As with the Alexa Tablet 11, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a fingerprint sensor. There's an anti-glare option that's said to preserve detail and color accuracy. It's called Nanomatte and if you want that on your tablet, that'll run you $50 extra. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is designed more for productivity. To that end, there are accessories such as the $90 Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and the $150 Alexa Tablet Pro Keyboard, which connects to the device magnetically. All of the tablets have Alexa+ baked in, of course. You can opt in to a feature that allows you to ask the assistant about whatever is displayed on your screen. Amazon designed the Kindle experience (the Kindle app is installed by default) to be distraction free with reduced blue light. The Nanomatte display is said to give ebooks a paper-like feel, and you can add notes to books using the Pro Pen. There are also Kids versions of the Alexa Tablet 8 and Alexa Tablet 11. Like the other Alexa tablets, these have an aluminum design but come with a "kid-proof case" to help protect them. These versions also come with one year of Amazon Kids+ access. As expected, Amazon has bid adieu to Fire OS . Alexa tablets run on Android 16 with a custom layer on top. As such, they offer direct access to the Google Play Store. As someone who had to jump through hoops to access apps outside of the limited selection that Amazon itself offered on Fire tablets, that's a very welcome change. Unfortunately, though, it appears that Alexa tablets do not have a microSD card slot you can use to expand the storage. Amazon has new dedicated reading devices as well . The latest standard Kindle starts at $150 and it costs an extra $20 to remove the lockscreen ads. The six-inch model is a millimeter thinner than the previous model at 6.8mm and it weighs five ounces. The screen is flush with the casing, which is available in a fetching purple called Ube as well as Graphite. Amazon says the new entry-level Kindle is 30 percent faster at opening books than the previous model and that it can run for six weeks on a charge. A variant with an aluminum casing and double the storage (32GB) will run you $190. This comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green color options. The latest Kindle Paperwhite has a seven-inch display, 16GB of storage, an adjustable warm light and what Amazon says is the highest contrast ratio on any Paperwhite to date. It's thinner and lighter than the previous model too. It costs $200, or $220 if you don't want lockscreen ads. Then there's the latest Paperwhite Signature Edition, which costs $250 and has no lockscreen ads, an aluminum back, 32GB of storage, auto-adjusting light and the option to double tap to turn pages. While the standard Paperwhite is only available in Graphite (also an option here), you can snag a Signature Edition in Seaglass Green. As for the updated Kindle Colorsoft, that has improved clarity and edge-to-edge color on the seven-inch display, Amazon says. Again, it's thinner and lighter than the previous model and there are no ads. The standard model with 16GB of storage is $290. The Colorsoft Signature Edition has an aluminum design, a Fig color option, 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light and a double-tap-to-turn-pages feature. That'll run you $320. Both Colorsoft variants run for up to eight weeks on a charge, according to Amazon. Kids versions of the ereaders are available too. They have kid-friendly covers and a year of access to Kids+. In addition, Ring has updated several of its cameras. The Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus and Indoor Cam 4K support Retinal 4K video capture . A new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K can rotate 360 degrees and tilt 175 degrees to automatically follow anything it detects to be moving. OK, Amazon announced this one in September , but isn't September 30 basically October? The company claims the new Fire TV Stick 4K is zippier than previous models. It says the device "turns on faster, apps launch over 35 percent faster, and content starts playing nearly 20 percent faster" than its predecessor and suggests it's faster than an unnamed rival dongle as well as some 4K smart TVs at playing content. This $60 Fire TV Stick 4K (Amazon wisely ditched the Select and Plus variants for this gen) is slimmer than earlier models and it can run on power from your TV's USB port. It has a 4-core processor, 8GB of storage, Alexa+ support and Wi-Fi 6. The company also redesigned the Fire TV remote. Bee announced its first two AI note-taking devices since Amazon bought the startup last year. The $75 Bee Frontier (which replaced the company's Pioneer model) is a Fitbit-esque wearable that has an estimated seven-day battery life and a IP67 rating for dust and water resistance. You can press a button to record audio of a conversation, and you can receive transcripts and summaries. If you hold the button, you can ask the AI assistant a question or create a voice note for yourself. Amazon says that, on Bee devices, "audio is never stored, cannot be accessed or shared, and users are prompted to gain permission from call participants each time a recording is started." As for the Bee Eclipse, that's a rectangular device that attaches to your phone magnetically. It has three microphones and a battery that's said to run for up to 21 days on a charge. Otherwise, it has much the same functionality as the Frontier. The Eclipse will run you $100 but, unlike the Frontier (which you can buy now), you'll have to wait for it. That device is "coming soon."

After years of teasers and warm-ups, Amazon finally pulled back the curtain on its new hardware lineup in New York. For a company that’s leaned so heavily on Alexa and its software smarts, the truth is that software only shines when the hardware around it does. Google has Nest. Apple has HomePods and Apple TVs. And Amazon? It’s long been the player trying to prove Alexa deserves a spot at the center of your living room. This year’s showcase felt different, more like Amazon finally putting its full hand on the table. The announcements went beyond shinier designs and brighter screens (though there was plenty of that). At the heart of it all was Alexa Plus , a new AI-powered assistant meant to tie the ecosystem together. From smarter speakers to larger displays to TVs that adapt to your space, here’s everything Amazon rolled out. Powered by Amazon’s AZ3 Pro chip, the new Echo Studio is tuned for sharper conversation detection and advanced AI models. It’s 40% smaller than the original but packs three full-range drivers, a custom woofer, and support for Dolby Atmos and spatial audio. For the first time, the light ring moves to the front. You can also connect up to five speakers with a Fire TV stick for what Amazon calls “Alexa Home Theater.” Price starts at $219.99, shipping October 29, with U.S. buyers getting early access to Alexa Plus–Amazon’s upgraded AI assistant. Alongside the Echo Studio comes the Echo Dot Max at $99.99, positioned directly against Apple’s HomePod Mini . The familiar sphere now has a flat face with controls and an LED ring. Inside, the AZ3 chip filters background noise, while a redesigned sound system delivers nearly three times the bass. It’s also the first Dot with two speakers: a high-excursion woofer and a tweeter. passages: With Alexa Tablets, revamped Kindles, upgraded Ring devices, refreshed Fire TV hardware and new AI-powered wearables already announced, Amazon’s fall product rollout is far from quiet.

The approach appears to align with the thinking of Panos Panay, Amazon’s head of Alexa and Devices, who recently suggested that large launch events often result in only a few products receiving meaningful attention while many others fade into the background.
Amazon also upgraded its streaming hardware lineup with a new Fire TV Stick 4K .
Amazon has also introduced children’s editions of the Alexa Tablet 8 and Alexa Tablet 11.

The broader theme running through every product launch is clear: Amazon is betting heavily on artificial intelligence, premium hardware experiences and deeper integration across its growing ecosystem of Alexa-powered devices.

It seems the company's chief of Alexa and devices Panos Panay might agree.

He recently told Engadget that "last year was a fine moment, but it turns out only two products really got any attention and everything else was just there." He also felt that the teams behind the overlooked products didn't get to take the pride that they, he felt, deserved.
Rather than hold a standard fall hardware event, Amazon has been announcing new products piecemeal over the last several weeks.
Bee announced its first two AI note-taking devices since Amazon bought the startup last year.

There’s also the new Echo Time smart alarm clock, the screenless Echo Studio with Home Camera, a fully redesigned Echo Dot, and Amazon’s latest flagship smart display, the Echo Show 16, which comes with a whopping eight woofers and can run the full Fire TV experience by touch.
Amazon had plenty of new gadgets to share at its Echo hardware event this year, along with updates to the AI-powered Alexa Plus after it became available to everyone in the US in February.
There’s the Alexa Photo Frame, which Amazon devices chief Panos Panay describes as “the world’s smartest photo frame” and that doubles as a full Alexa speaker.

Amazon’s 2025 fall showcase wasn’t just about rolling out shinier gadgets; it was about showing how Alexa Plus now runs through everything, from the speakers on your shelf to the TV in your living room, the Kindle in your bag, and the cameras on your front door.
By blending hardware upgrades with AI smarts, Amazon is betting big on keeping its devices at the centre of your home life.
After years of teasers and warm-ups, Amazon finally pulled back the curtain on its new hardware lineup in New York.
From smarter speakers to larger displays to TVs that adapt to your space, here’s everything Amazon rolled out.

With Alexa Tablets, revamped Kindles, upgraded Ring devices, refreshed Fire TV hardware and new AI-powered wearables already announced, Amazon’s fall product rollout is far from quiet.

The approach appears to align with the thinking of Panos Panay, Amazon’s head of Alexa and Devices, who recently suggested that large launch events often result in only a few products receiving meaningful attention while many others fade into the background.
Amazon also upgraded its streaming hardware lineup with a new Fire TV Stick 4K .
Amazon has also introduced children’s editions of the Alexa Tablet 8 and Alexa Tablet 11.

The broader theme running through every product launch is clear: Amazon is betting heavily on artificial intelligence, premium hardware experiences and deeper integration across its growing ecosystem of Alexa-powered devices.

Instead of hosting a traditional fall hardware event packed with dozens of announcements at once, Amazon has taken a different approach this year, unveiling new products gradually over several weeks .
The strategy has allowed each product to enjoy its own spotlight while keeping Amazon consistently in the tech conversation throughout October.
Amazon has officially retired Fire OS in favor of Android 16 with a custom Amazon interface layered on top.

The company has unveiled an all-new lineup of Alexa Tablets , which feature a more premium design, stronger specifications, built-in AI features and, perhaps most importantly, direct access to the Google Play Store.
Amazon describes it as its most powerful tablet ever, claiming:
Amazon says audio recorded through Bee devices is not permanently stored and users are prompted to obtain participant consent whenever recordings begin.
To support that goal, Amazon has introduced new accessories including:
Interestingly, Amazon appears to have dropped microSD card support, meaning storage expansion may no longer be possible.
Priced at $75 , the Bee Frontier is a wearable device resembling a fitness tracker.
The inclusion of a dedicated neural processing unit allows the tablet to handle certain AI tasks directly on the device, reducing reliance on cloud-based computing.
For many users, this addresses one of the biggest limitations that affected previous Fire tablets.
Amazon-owned Ring is expanding beyond cameras and video doorbells.
