Siri AI can draw on personal context to help pros find what they need in the moment across messages, emails, photos, and more; answer questions about virtually any topic; and get things done across apps — all with groundbreaking privacy protections. extraction.body: ElevenLabs , an AI startup that just raised a $180 million mega-funding round , has been primarily known for its audio-generation prowess. The company took a step in another technological direction by launching its first stand-alone speech-to-text model called Scribe. The startup, valued at $3.3 billion , has aided many other companies in providing text-to-speech services through its vast library of voices. However, the company is now looking to get into speech detection and compete with the likes of Gladia , Speechmatics , AssemblyAI , Deepgram , and OpenAI's Whisper models. ElevenLabs' Scribe model supports over 99 languages at launch. The company categorizes over 25 languages in excellent accuracy category for the model where the word error rate is less than 5%. This list includes English (claimed accuracy rate of 97%), French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Japanese, Kannada, Malayalam, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish, and Vietnamese. Other languages are ranked in different categories with high (5% to 10% word error rate), good (10% to 20% word error rate), and moderate (25% to 50%) word error rates. The company said that the model outperformed Google Gemini 2.0 Flash and Whisper Large V3 across multiple languages in FLEURS & Common Voice benchmark tests. ElevenLabs had developed the speech-to-text component for its AI conversational agent platform, which was released last year. However, this is the first time the company is releasing a stand-alone speech detection model . In a conversation with TechCrunch last month, CEO Mati Staniszewski talked about improving speech detection models. "We want to understand what's being said by you in a conversation better. We are working on ways to move away from only generating content and understanding and transcribing speech," Staniszewski said at that time. "Many people say that speech-to-text is a solved problem. But for many languages, it is pretty bad. We think we can build better speech detection models because we have in-house teams to annotate data and give us quick feedback." The model also has smart speaker diarization to tell you who is speaking, timestamp at word level for accurate subtitles, and auto-tagging sound events like audience laughters. The startup is providing a way for customers to directly transcribe video content to add subtitles or captions in its studio. Scribe currently only works with pre-recorded audio formats. The company said it will release a low-latency real-time version of the model soon. That means it is not yet effective for meeting transcriptions or voice note-taking. ElevenLabs is pricing Scribe at $0.40 for an hour of transcribed audio. While the rate is competitive, some of its rivals offer a lower price for audio transcriptions at the moment with some feature differentiation.

extraction.body: NVIDIA released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on October 28, 2026. It is an open speech model that handles transcription, speaker attribution, translation and audio question answering in one set of weights. Coverage from SiliconANGLE, TechCrunch, AI Insider and Technology Org put the launch at the top of today’s AI news. The pitch is simple. Instead of chaining a speech recognizer, a diarization tool, a translation engine and a text model, a developer points one model at an audio file and tells it what to do in plain language. The reports describe a single model that covers 40 languages for transcription, 31 languages for translation to or from English, and speaker attribution in 13 languages. This piece sorts what the announcement confirms from what it leaves open. It also places the release next to NVIDIA’s earlier Nemotron 3.5 open models and the wider fight over open-weight AI. The Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe name matters here, because the “all-in-one adaptable” wording floating around headlines is not confirmed as official NVIDIA language. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The official product name found in the reporting is NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe. NVIDIA describes it as an open speech LLM built for intelligent transcription. In practice that means an open-weight model that listens to audio and produces text, but also reasons about what it heard. The “speech LLM” label is the key. Classic automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems turn sound into words and stop there. A speech LLM accepts audio as input to a language model, which lets it follow instructions. Ask it for a verbatim transcript and it keeps the stumbles and filler words. Ask for written form and it cleans the text up. Ask a question about the recording and it answers. Every figure below comes from the verified launch details. Anything the sources do not state, such as accuracy scores, parameter counts or licensing terms, stays out of the table on purpose. Read the three language counts together. Forty languages for plain transcription is the widest net. Translation narrows to 31 languages, and every one of those pairs touches English. Speaker attribution narrows again to 13. The model does more in some languages than in others, and buyers should plan around that gradient. The headline capability is consolidation. NVIDIA says one model covers four jobs that teams usually split across separate tools. Those jobs are transcription, speaker attribution, translation and question answering over audio. Transcription style is a real product decision. A court reporter wants every false start preserved. A podcast editor wants a clean paragraph. Most speech systems force that choice at build time through separate models or post-processing rules. According to the reports, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe makes it a runtime instruction, so the same weights serve both audiences. Speaker attribution answers the question of who said what. The model identifies up to eight speakers in a recording and supports this in 13 languages. Word timestamps tie each word to a position in the audio, which makes it possible to jump from a transcript line straight to the sound, build subtitles, or search a long meeting. What a unified model does offer with certainty is fewer moving parts. One deployment, one set of weights to version, one failure surface to monitor. For small teams that alone can decide the build-versus-buy math. The language numbers deserve a slower read than the headline gives them. A claim of 40 languages tells you the model can transcribe in 40. It does not tell you the quality is equal across all of them, and the sources publish no per-language accuracy figures. Translation is anchored on English. The 31 languages are described as to or from English, so a Spanish-to-Japanese request would not be a listed direction. Teams that need direct pairs would have to route through English, which can compound errors, or test the model themselves. Speaker attribution is the narrowest at 13 languages. If your audio is Hindi, Swahili or Vietnamese, check the model card before you promise speaker labels to a customer. Transcription may work while attribution does not. Voice products in fast-growing markets feel this gap most. Our earlier look at India’s voice AI latency budget shows how tight real-time speech constraints get once multilingual audio enters the picture. The reports say the model handles recordings up to one hour and identifies up to eight speakers. Those are practical limits, and they map neatly onto real workloads. A board meeting, a lecture, a podcast episode or a customer call all fit inside an hour. A full-day deposition or a conference keynote with a long Q&A does not. None of this is a flaw, just a boundary. Stating the ceiling openly helps teams scope pilots honestly. A model that promises unlimited length usually hides its limits in quality drift. A model with a stated one-hour cap at least tells you where to look. The sources list no price for Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe. That is consistent with an open-weight release distributed through Hugging Face and ModelScope, where the model files are the product. The cited reports do not spell out the license, so check the model card for commercial-use terms before you build on it. Open weights shift cost from a per-minute API bill to your own compute. A team running thousands of hours of audio a month can trade a recurring vendor invoice for GPU time it already owns. A team with a few hours of audio a month may still prefer a hosted API, since idle GPUs cost money too. Education and enterprise meetings. Lectures and team calls fit inside the one-hour cap. Searchable, speaker-labeled transcripts with translation help multilingual classrooms and global teams. NVIDIA enters a crowded field. OpenAI open-sourced Whisper in 2022, and that release made open-weight transcription a baseline expectation. Cloud providers sell managed speech APIs with transcription, diarization and translation as separate or bundled features. Specialist vendors compete on accuracy and latency. NVIDIA’s own earlier speech work, including its Parakeet and Canary model families, also shaped expectations before this launch. The new angle is bundling. Whisper-style models transcribe and translate but leave speaker attribution to add-on tools. Managed clouds bundle features, but behind a per-minute meter and a data-sharing agreement. A single open model that does all four jobs, at least on paper, targets the gap between those two options. The broader open-weight race adds pressure. Chinese labs have pushed hard on open releases, a trend we tracked in our DeepSeek, Qwen and Mistral comparison . NVIDIA’s decision to list the model on ModelScope as well as Hugging Face suggests it wants a seat in that ecosystem too. For more on how these model families stack up, see the AI and machine learning section . For buyers, the comparison comes down to four questions. Does the model cover your languages, including speaker attribution? Does the license allow your use? Does it run on hardware you can afford? And does it beat your current setup on your own audio? Only the first question has a partial answer today, because the reports confirm the language counts. The other three depend on the model card and on testing. Speech recognition spent decades as a pipeline problem. Acoustic models, pronunciation dictionaries and language models sat in separate components. Deep learning collapsed those into end-to-end networks, and large-scale training on web audio then pushed accuracy up sharply, which is why Whisper in 2022 felt like a turning point for open tools. The next shift joined speech to large language models. Once a language model can ingest audio, it can follow instructions about that audio. Transcription becomes one skill among several rather than the whole product. That is the lineage Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe belongs to, and the “speech LLM” label in the reporting points straight at it. The Nemotron name itself carries history. NVIDIA has used it for a line of open models, and the 3.5 label ties this speech release to that family. Our earlier report on the Nemotron 3.5 open models covers the family’s other releases, so a speech member arriving now fits a pattern of NVIDIA widening its open lineup. The sources do not describe how the speech model was trained or how it relates to its siblings, so that connection stays at the level of naming and timing. Seen that way, the release is less a leap than a consolidation. The ingredients existed in separate tools. NVIDIA packaged them into one open model and put it where developers already shop for weights. Launch-day coverage tends to blur the line between announced and verified. Here is where this story stands. The “all-in-one adaptable” phrasing is a reporter’s shorthand, not a verified NVIDIA tagline. The model also has no “Nemotron 3.5 audio transcription and translation model” title. The official name is NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, and readers searching for it should use that. Several questions remain after launch day, and a careful team will answer them before committing. These are analyst judgments, not reported facts, and the sources do not back any of them. What is NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe? It is an open speech LLM from NVIDIA, released October 28, 2026, that handles transcription, speaker attribution, translation and audio question answering in one model. It is an open speech model that handles transcription, speaker attribution, translation and audio question answering in one set of weights. Coverage from SiliconANGLE, TechCrunch, AI Insider and Technology Org put the launch at the top of today’s AI news.

The pitch is simple. Instead of chaining a speech recognizer, a diarization tool, a translation engine and a text model, a developer points one model at an audio file and tells it what to do in plain language. The reports describe a single model that covers 40 languages for transcription, 31 languages for translation to or from English, and speaker attribution in 13 languages.

This piece sorts what the announcement confirms from what it leaves open. It also places the release next to NVIDIA’s earlier Nemotron 3.5 open models and the wider fight over open-weight AI. The Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe name matters here, because the “all-in-one adaptable” wording floating around headlines is not confirmed as official NVIDIA language.
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

The official product name found in the reporting is NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe. NVIDIA describes it as an open speech LLM built for intelligent transcription. In practice that means an open-weight model that listens to audio and produces text, but also reasons about what it heard.

The “speech LLM” label is the key. Classic automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems turn sound into words and stop there. A speech LLM accepts audio as input to a language model, which lets it follow instructions. Ask it for a verbatim transcript and it keeps the stumbles and filler words. Ask for written form and it cleans the text up. Ask a question about the recording and it answers.
Every figure below comes from the verified launch details. Anything the sources do not state, such as accuracy scores, parameter counts or licensing terms, stays out of the table on purpose.

Read the three language counts together. Forty languages for plain transcription is the widest net. Translation narrows to 31 languages, and every one of those pairs touches English. Speaker attribution narrows again to 13. The model does more in some languages than in others, and buyers should plan around that gradient.

The headline capability is consolidation. NVIDIA says one model covers four jobs that teams usually split across separate tools. Those jobs are transcription, speaker attribution, translation and question answering over audio.

Transcription style is a real product decision. A court reporter wants every false start preserved. A podcast editor wants a clean paragraph. Most speech systems force that choice at build time through separate models or post-processing rules. According to the reports, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe makes it a runtime instruction, so the same weights serve both audiences.

Speaker attribution answers the question of who said what. The model identifies up to eight speakers in a recording and supports this in 13 languages. Word timestamps tie each word to a position in the audio, which makes it possible to jump from a transcript line straight to the sound, build subtitles, or search a long meeting.

What a unified model does offer with certainty is fewer moving parts. One deployment, one set of weights to version, one failure surface to monitor. For small teams that alone can decide the build-versus-buy math.

The language numbers deserve a slower read than the headline gives them. A claim of 40 languages tells you the model can transcribe in 40. It does not tell you the quality is equal across all of them, and the sources publish no per-language accuracy figures.

Translation is anchored on English. The 31 languages are described as to or from English, so a Spanish-to-Japanese request would not be a listed direction. Teams that need direct pairs would have to route through English, which can compound errors, or test the model themselves.

Speaker attribution is the narrowest at 13 languages. If your audio is Hindi, Swahili or Vietnamese, check the model card before you promise speaker labels to a customer. Transcription may work while attribution does not. Voice products in fast-growing markets feel this gap most. Our earlier look at India’s voice AI latency budget shows how tight real-time speech constraints get once multilingual audio enters the picture.

The reports say the model handles recordings up to one hour and identifies up to eight speakers. Those are practical limits, and they map neatly onto real workloads. A board meeting, a lecture, a podcast episode or a customer call all fit inside an hour. A full-day deposition or a conference keynote with a long Q&A does not.

None of this is a flaw, just a boundary. Stating the ceiling openly helps teams scope pilots honestly. A model that promises unlimited length usually hides its limits in quality drift. A model with a stated one-hour cap at least tells you where to look.

The sources list no price for Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe. That is consistent with an open-weight release distributed through Hugging Face and ModelScope, where the model files are the product. The cited reports do not spell out the license, so check the model card for commercial-use terms before you build on it.

Open weights shift cost from a per-minute API bill to your own compute. A team running thousands of hours of audio a month can trade a recurring vendor invoice for GPU time it already owns. A team with a few hours of audio a month may still prefer a hosted API, since idle GPUs cost money too.
Education and enterprise meetings. Lectures and team calls fit inside the one-hour cap. Searchable, speaker-labeled transcripts with translation help multilingual classrooms and global teams.

NVIDIA enters a crowded field. OpenAI open-sourced Whisper in 2022, and that release made open-weight transcription a baseline expectation. Cloud providers sell managed speech APIs with transcription, diarization and translation as separate or bundled features. Specialist vendors compete on accuracy and latency. NVIDIA’s own earlier speech work, including its Parakeet and Canary model families, also shaped expectations before this launch.

The new angle is bundling. Whisper-style models transcribe and translate but leave speaker attribution to add-on tools. Managed clouds bundle features, but behind a per-minute meter and a data-sharing agreement. A single open model that does all four jobs, at least on paper, targets the gap between those two options.

The broader open-weight race adds pressure. Chinese labs have pushed hard on open releases, a trend we tracked in our DeepSeek, Qwen and Mistral comparison . NVIDIA’s decision to list the model on ModelScope as well as Hugging Face suggests it wants a seat in that ecosystem too. For more on how these model families stack up, see the AI and machine learning section .

For buyers, the comparison comes down to four questions. Does the model cover your languages, including speaker attribution? Does the license allow your use? Does it run on hardware you can afford? And does it beat your current setup on your own audio? Only the first question has a partial answer today, because the reports confirm the language counts. The other three depend on the model card and on testing.

Speech recognition spent decades as a pipeline problem. Acoustic models, pronunciation dictionaries and language models sat in separate components. Deep learning collapsed those into end-to-end networks, and large-scale training on web audio then pushed accuracy up sharply, which is why Whisper in 2022 felt like a turning point for open tools.

The next shift joined speech to large language models. Once a language model can ingest audio, it can follow instructions about that audio. Transcription becomes one skill among several rather than the whole product. That is the lineage Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe belongs to, and the “speech LLM” label in the reporting points straight at it.

The Nemotron name itself carries history. NVIDIA has used it for a line of open models, and the 3.5 label ties this speech release to that family. Our earlier report on the Nemotron 3.5 open models covers the family’s other releases, so a speech member arriving now fits a pattern of NVIDIA widening its open lineup. The sources do not describe how the speech model was trained or how it relates to its siblings, so that connection stays at the level of naming and timing.

Seen that way, the release is less a leap than a consolidation. The ingredients existed in separate tools. NVIDIA packaged them into one open model and put it where developers already shop for weights.

coreStoryFacts.text: ElevenLabs , an AI startup that just raised a $180 million mega-funding round , has been primarily known for its audio-generation prowess.
The company took a step in another technological direction by launching its first stand-alone speech-to-text model called Scribe.
In a conversation with TechCrunch last month, CEO Mati Staniszewski talked about improving speech detection models.
ElevenLabs' Scribe model supports over 99 languages at launch.
The company categorizes over 25 languages in excellent accuracy category for the model where the word error rate is less than 5%.
This list includes English (claimed accuracy rate of 97%), French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Japanese, Kannada, Malayalam, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish, and Vietnamese.
ElevenLabs is pricing Scribe at $0.40 for an hour of transcribed audio.
While the rate is competitive, some of its rivals offer a lower price for audio transcriptions at the moment with some feature differentiation.
The startup, valued at $3.3 billion , has aided many other companies in providing text-to-speech services through its vast library of voices.

Still, the company promises Transcribe, at 30 billion parameters, can run on a single chip, from the Jetson AGX Thor robotics controller and DGX Spark chip powering new laptops , to Blackwell datacenter chips.
It joins Nvidia’s open-weight voice models, including the super small yet powerful Parakeet (1.1 billion parameters).
Nvidia on Wednesday released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe , a free, open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages.
It also released version 2 of Granary, its open source speech dataset.
These tools target developers building apps for business meetings and medical transcription, two of AI’s most established footholds in the workplace.
Nvidia says developers can use the model, the updated Granary dataset, and tools like its NeMo Speech model to customize apps to recognize an industry’s jargon in each language.
One drawback: Transcribe works with recorded audio, not livestreams.

Speech recognition spent decades as a pipeline problem. Acoustic models, pronunciation dictionaries and language models sat in separate components. extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing.

sources.title: Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a DHS Data Leak Exposing 41,000 Workers And Undercover ICE Agents - International Business Times, Singapore Edition
passages: Bluesky is blocking links to a leaked archive containing records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including personnel connected to undercover operations.

The archive, called Icepick, contains information associated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

In 2020, Twitter suspended DDoSecrets' account and blocked links to its website after the organization published BlueLeaks, a large collection of internal records from police agencies and fusion centers.
Bluesky said it chose to block links rather than remove posts discussing the leak, aiming to avoid restricting public discussion or access to reporting and commentary.
Users who try to open Icepick links through Bluesky's website or app encounter a "Blocked Link" page identifying the URL as malicious.

extraction.body: Bluesky is blocking links to a leaked archive containing records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including personnel connected to undercover operations. The archive, called Icepick, contains information associated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The social media platform told WIRED it restricted the links because the archive contains contact information shared without authorization. The decision allows users to discuss the leak while limiting direct access to the exposed records, raising questions about how platforms should balance government accountability with the privacy and safety of public employees. Users who try to open Icepick links through Bluesky's website or app encounter a "Blocked Link" page identifying the URL as malicious. Bluesky said it chose to block links rather than remove posts discussing the leak, aiming to avoid restricting public discussion or access to reporting and commentary. The restriction also applies to a searchable website created by researcher and journalist Maia Arson Crimew. The block is not universal. The Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) homepage remains accessible through Bluesky, and the third-party app Klearsky reportedly opens the archive links without displaying a warning. The company has not said whether the restriction was applied automatically or whether a government agency requested it. The archive reportedly contains names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, office locations and internal group memberships. These details could reveal how DHS is organized, who works in particular units and which personnel have access to certain technologies or programs. A group calling itself the Department of Peace claims it obtained the records through DHS's Okta single sign-on service. DDoSecrets published the material after receiving it from the group. Okta disputed the suggestion that its own systems had been compromised. "We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised," the company told WIRED. That statement does not establish how the records were obtained. Reuters could not authenticate the entire dataset, although it corroborated some employee details and confirmed information directly with three DHS staff members. The leak includes information that may identify personnel connected to undercover work, surveillance and other sensitive operations. However, the full extent of the exposure remains uncertain, and the available reporting does not establish that every person associated with such operations has been identified or that a specific operation has been compromised. The group behind the release has framed it as a response to government data collection. An accompanying note argues that because the government holds information about members of the public, releasing information about government personnel is fair in return. Supporters of publishing the records argue that information about the people and systems behind immigration enforcement and surveillance could help journalists investigate government activities and support public oversight. But exposing personnel records carries risks beyond scrutiny of official conduct. Contact details and job assignments could make employees easier to target with harassment, threats or impersonation. Information about sensitive roles could also put investigations or personnel at risk. Bluesky's approach draws a line between discussing the leak and directly distributing the archive. Its community guidelines restrict the sharing of personal contact information but also protect factual reporting on matters of public interest, including government transparency and public officials. DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best said social platforms have previously restricted access to the organization's publications. "They can't stop the signal," Best told WIRED. Bluesky's decision has a precedent. In 2020, Twitter suspended DDoSecrets' account and blocked links to its website after the organization published BlueLeaks, a large collection of internal records from police agencies and fusion centers. The current restriction of Bluesky is blocking links to the specific DHS archive while leaving its homepage and discussion of the leak accessible. However, the approach raises questions about how platforms distinguish the distribution of exposed personal information from legitimate reporting about the same material. Blocking an archive can limit access to sensitive records, but it can also affect journalists and researchers who want to examine information relevant to government accountability. For now, Bluesky says its restriction is intended to limit the spread of unauthorized contact information without silencing broader discussion. The full extent of the leak remains unclear, and neither the complete dataset nor its claimed source has been independently verified.

The information included “more than 21,000” agents working for CBP and “Nearly 6,600” working for ICE, and other records covered Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service, and people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The breach raised “broad security concerns” and described fears that adversarial actors could misuse the data for targeted personal attacks or to blackmail government employees.

A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online. The information included “more than 21,000” agents working for CBP and “Nearly 6,600” working for ICE, and other records covered Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service, and people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The Guardian said the records were made public by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and that they revealed “operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives.” Records include references to surveillance tools like PenLink. Emma Best described the search tool as replacing anonymity with accountability, and it quoted her saying the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability.” Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim that Department of Peace harvested the data from Okta, and Okta responded to a Reuters query with “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.” The leaked information included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir. The groups wrote in an online statement that the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent, and it quoted Emma Best saying the leak was extraordinary but deceptive because it identifies officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations. The breach raised “broad security concerns” and described fears that adversarial actors could misuse the data for targeted personal attacks or to blackmail government employees. The disclosure revealed how the agency is organized and included job titles and email groups that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. The entity known as the Ministry of Peace said DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” and it said the entity hoped the data would be used to “mitigate further damage that the department may cause.” whether the hacker groups' stated intent is treated as credible New leak shakes the internal security of the United States.. The leak includes agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency, and it identified the database as Icepick.

Emma Best described the search tool as replacing anonymity with accountability, and it quoted her saying the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability.” Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim that Department of Peace harvested the data from Okta, and Okta responded to a Reuters query with “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”

The breach raised “broad security concerns” and described fears that adversarial actors could misuse the data for targeted personal attacks or to blackmail government employees.

The disclosure revealed how the agency is organized and included job titles and email groups that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work. sources.title: Massive DHS Data Breach Raises Fears for Undercover ICE Agents as Sensitive Operations Are Exposed
passages: These records offer a broader picture of the department's organisational structure than a conventional staff directory, potentially exposing connections between personnel and the systems they use.Reuters reported that it could not authenticate the entire dataset, although it corroborated some employee information through independent checks and direct contact with DHS staff.Undercover ICE Agents and Surveillance Work IdentifiedWIRED's analysis found records associated with personnel involved in undercover operations, wiretaps and surveillance programmes.

More than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors have reportedly had their professional details exposed in a major data leak, raising concerns about undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel and sensitive surveillance operations.The leaked records reportedly include contact information, job titles and internal access groups, potentially revealing how personnel and systems across multiple federal agencies are connected.DHS Data Leak Exposes More Than 41,000 WorkersThe archive, known as 'Icepick,' was published by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets on 28 October.

Some entries reportedly identify groups linked to investigative software, immigration databases and tools used to analyse telephone records and social media activity.The dataset also reportedly includes personnel connected to Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition application used by immigration agents, as well as accounts associated with encrypted messaging services.The exposure of such information could create security risks if outsiders use it to identify personnel, impersonate officials or infer relationships between investigators and their operations.

Information about professional relationships and access permissions could also help outsiders better understand the department's internal operations.Homeland Security Responds To Reported Data LeakDHS acknowledged a potential breach and said it was working to address the situation and protect employees, according to Reuters.

According to WIRED, many records identify supervisors, while access groups reveal links between staff members and particular tools or programmes.Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, warned WIRED that the dataset could become more valuable when combined with other compromised information.

extraction.body: More than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors have reportedly had their professional details exposed in a major data leak, raising concerns about undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel and sensitive surveillance operations.The leaked records reportedly include contact information, job titles and internal access groups, potentially revealing how personnel and systems across multiple federal agencies are connected.DHS Data Leak Exposes More Than 41,000 WorkersThe archive, known as 'Icepick,' was published by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets on 28 October. WIRED reported that the records cover DHS and seven component agencies, including ICE, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.The information includes names, email addresses, telephone numbers, office locations, job titles and details about employees' supervisors and internal access groups. These records offer a broader picture of the department's organisational structure than a conventional staff directory, potentially exposing connections between personnel and the systems they use.Reuters reported that it could not authenticate the entire dataset, although it corroborated some employee information through independent checks and direct contact with DHS staff.Undercover ICE Agents and Surveillance Work IdentifiedWIRED's analysis found records associated with personnel involved in undercover operations, wiretaps and surveillance programmes. Some entries reportedly identify groups linked to investigative software, immigration databases and tools used to analyse telephone records and social media activity.The dataset also reportedly includes personnel connected to Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition application used by immigration agents, as well as accounts associated with encrypted messaging services.The exposure of such information could create security risks if outsiders use it to identify personnel, impersonate officials or infer relationships between investigators and their operations. However, the publication of employee records does not automatically mean that active investigations have been compromised or that undercover identities have been conclusively exposed.DHS Data Leak Raises Internal Security ConcernsThe reported leak could provide insight into how DHS organises access to internal systems and distributes responsibilities among employees and contractors. According to WIRED, many records identify supervisors, while access groups reveal links between staff members and particular tools or programmes.Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, warned WIRED that the dataset could become more valuable when combined with other compromised information. Such cross-referencing could help malicious actors develop convincing impersonation attempts or identify vulnerable personnel.The potential consequences therefore extend beyond the exposure of telephone numbers and email addresses. Information about professional relationships and access permissions could also help outsiders better understand the department's internal operations.Homeland Security Responds To Reported Data LeakDHS acknowledged a potential breach and said it was working to address the situation and protect employees, according to Reuters. The department also said it would provide further information when more details became available.The circumstances surrounding the alleged breach remain disputed. Distributed Denial of Secrets said the records were obtained from an entity calling itself the Department of Peace, which claimed responsibility for the disclosure. The organisation said the release was intended to promote accountability and support public scrutiny of government activities.The group claimed the information originated from DHS' Okta sign-on service. Okta said it had no evidence that its systems or data had been compromised.The full extent of the exposure, including whether any active investigations or undercover operations have been affected, remains unclear.

Bluesky is blocking links to a leaked archive containing records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including personnel connected to undercover operations.

The archive, called Icepick, contains information associated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

Bluesky said it chose to block links rather than remove posts discussing the leak, aiming to avoid restricting public discussion or access to reporting and commentary.
Users who try to open Icepick links through Bluesky's website or app encounter a "Blocked Link" page identifying the URL as malicious.

extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. More than 100 HSI agents, including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing.

extraction.body: Bluesky is blocking links to a leaked archive containing records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including personnel connected to undercover operations. The archive, called Icepick, contains information associated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The social media platform told WIRED it restricted the links because the archive contains contact information shared without authorization. The decision allows users to discuss the leak while limiting direct access to the exposed records, raising questions about how platforms should balance government accountability with the privacy and safety of public employees. Users who try to open Icepick links through Bluesky's website or app encounter a "Blocked Link" page identifying the URL as malicious. Bluesky said it chose to block links rather than remove posts discussing the leak, aiming to avoid restricting public discussion or access to reporting and commentary. The restriction also applies to a searchable website created by researcher and journalist Maia Arson Crimew. The block is not universal. The Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) homepage remains accessible through Bluesky, and the third-party app Klearsky reportedly opens the archive links without displaying a warning. The company has not said whether the restriction was applied automatically or whether a government agency requested it. The archive reportedly contains names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, office locations and internal group memberships. These details could reveal how DHS is organized, who works in particular units and which personnel have access to certain technologies or programs. A group calling itself the Department of Peace claims it obtained the records through DHS's Okta single sign-on service. DDoSecrets published the material after receiving it from the group. Okta disputed the suggestion that its own systems had been compromised. "We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised," the company told WIRED. That statement does not establish how the records were obtained. Reuters could not authenticate the entire dataset, although it corroborated some employee details and confirmed information directly with three DHS staff members. The leak includes information that may identify personnel connected to undercover work, surveillance and other sensitive operations. However, the full extent of the exposure remains uncertain, and the available reporting does not establish that every person associated with such operations has been identified or that a specific operation has been compromised. The group behind the release has framed it as a response to government data collection. An accompanying note argues that because the government holds information about members of the public, releasing information about government personnel is fair in return. Supporters of publishing the records argue that information about the people and systems behind immigration enforcement and surveillance could help journalists investigate government activities and support public oversight. But exposing personnel records carries risks beyond scrutiny of official conduct. Contact details and job assignments could make employees easier to target with harassment, threats or impersonation. Information about sensitive roles could also put investigations or personnel at risk. Bluesky's approach draws a line between discussing the leak and directly distributing the archive. Its community guidelines restrict the sharing of personal contact information but also protect factual reporting on matters of public interest, including government transparency and public officials. DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best said social platforms have previously restricted access to the organization's publications. "They can't stop the signal," Best told WIRED. Bluesky's decision has a precedent. In 2020, Twitter suspended DDoSecrets' account and blocked links to its website after the organization published BlueLeaks, a large collection of internal records from police agencies and fusion centers. The current restriction of Bluesky is blocking links to the specific DHS archive while leaving its homepage and discussion of the leak accessible. However, the approach raises questions about how platforms distinguish the distribution of exposed personal information from legitimate reporting about the same material. Blocking an archive can limit access to sensitive records, but it can also affect journalists and researchers who want to examine information relevant to government accountability. For now, Bluesky says its restriction is intended to limit the spread of unauthorized contact information without silencing broader discussion. The full extent of the leak remains unclear, and neither the complete dataset nor its claimed source has been independently verified.

passages: These records offer a broader picture of the department's organisational structure than a conventional staff directory, potentially exposing connections between personnel and the systems they use.Reuters reported that it could not authenticate the entire dataset, although it corroborated some employee information through independent checks and direct contact with DHS staff.Undercover ICE Agents and Surveillance Work IdentifiedWIRED's analysis found records associated with personnel involved in undercover operations, wiretaps and surveillance programmes.

More than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors have reportedly had their professional details exposed in a major data leak, raising concerns about undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel and sensitive surveillance operations.The leaked records reportedly include contact information, job titles and internal access groups, potentially revealing how personnel and systems across multiple federal agencies are connected.DHS Data Leak Exposes More Than 41,000 WorkersThe archive, known as 'Icepick,' was published by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets on 28 October.

Some entries reportedly identify groups linked to investigative software, immigration databases and tools used to analyse telephone records and social media activity.The dataset also reportedly includes personnel connected to Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition application used by immigration agents, as well as accounts associated with encrypted messaging services.The exposure of such information could create security risks if outsiders use it to identify personnel, impersonate officials or infer relationships between investigators and their operations.

Information about professional relationships and access permissions could also help outsiders better understand the department's internal operations.Homeland Security Responds To Reported Data LeakDHS acknowledged a potential breach and said it was working to address the situation and protect employees, according to Reuters.

According to WIRED, many records identify supervisors, while access groups reveal links between staff members and particular tools or programmes.Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, warned WIRED that the dataset could become more valuable when combined with other compromised information.

extraction.body: More than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors have reportedly had their professional details exposed in a major data leak, raising concerns about undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel and sensitive surveillance operations.The leaked records reportedly include contact information, job titles and internal access groups, potentially revealing how personnel and systems across multiple federal agencies are connected.DHS Data Leak Exposes More Than 41,000 WorkersThe archive, known as 'Icepick,' was published by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets on 28 October. WIRED reported that the records cover DHS and seven component agencies, including ICE, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.The information includes names, email addresses, telephone numbers, office locations, job titles and details about employees' supervisors and internal access groups. These records offer a broader picture of the department's organisational structure than a conventional staff directory, potentially exposing connections between personnel and the systems they use.Reuters reported that it could not authenticate the entire dataset, although it corroborated some employee information through independent checks and direct contact with DHS staff.Undercover ICE Agents and Surveillance Work IdentifiedWIRED's analysis found records associated with personnel involved in undercover operations, wiretaps and surveillance programmes. Some entries reportedly identify groups linked to investigative software, immigration databases and tools used to analyse telephone records and social media activity.The dataset also reportedly includes personnel connected to Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition application used by immigration agents, as well as accounts associated with encrypted messaging services.The exposure of such information could create security risks if outsiders use it to identify personnel, impersonate officials or infer relationships between investigators and their operations. However, the publication of employee records does not automatically mean that active investigations have been compromised or that undercover identities have been conclusively exposed.DHS Data Leak Raises Internal Security ConcernsThe reported leak could provide insight into how DHS organises access to internal systems and distributes responsibilities among employees and contractors. According to WIRED, many records identify supervisors, while access groups reveal links between staff members and particular tools or programmes.Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, warned WIRED that the dataset could become more valuable when combined with other compromised information. Such cross-referencing could help malicious actors develop convincing impersonation attempts or identify vulnerable personnel.The potential consequences therefore extend beyond the exposure of telephone numbers and email addresses. Information about professional relationships and access permissions could also help outsiders better understand the department's internal operations.Homeland Security Responds To Reported Data LeakDHS acknowledged a potential breach and said it was working to address the situation and protect employees, according to Reuters. The department also said it would provide further information when more details became available.The circumstances surrounding the alleged breach remain disputed. Distributed Denial of Secrets said the records were obtained from an entity calling itself the Department of Peace, which claimed responsibility for the disclosure. The organisation said the release was intended to promote accountability and support public scrutiny of government activities.The group claimed the information originated from DHS' Okta sign-on service. Okta said it had no evidence that its systems or data had been compromised.The full extent of the exposure, including whether any active investigations or undercover operations have been affected, remains unclear.

Developers disclosed three vulnerabilities on October 28, following AI-assisted security research by Project Loupe. The disclosures arrived just hours after the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady, leaving holders focused on Friday's $12 billion Bitcoin options expiry. The vulnerabilities affect Bitcoin Core, the software used by nodes to verify transactions and enforce Bitcoin's rules. One flaw could allow malicious peers to crash nodes running Windows, macOS, and BSD. Another could gradually exhaust memory, while a third could corrupt blockchain undo data under extreme conditions. Bitcoin Core developers have already released fixes across four maintained release branches. However, the timing puts network security alongside monetary policy and derivatives positioning in an unusually busy week. DISCOVER: 15+ Best Crypto IPO to Watch in 2026 The most serious of the three disclosed issues involves unbounded memory growth through TCP urgent data. A malicious peer could bypass normal memory protections and overwhelm vulnerable nodes running non-Linux operating systems. This flaw does not affect Linux nodes. A second vulnerability allows memory usage to grow gradually when a peer pretends to use an older Bitcoin protocol. The attacker can exploit weaknesses in message queuing and connection handling to keep accumulating data. Bitcoin Core estimates growth of up to 2 MB per hour per inbound peer and 5 MB per hour per outbound peer. The third issue concerns oversized undo files, which store information needed to disconnect blocks during reorganizations. Under extreme conditions, a miner could create valid blocks that push an undo file beyond 4 GB. The resulting corruption could cause affected nodes to shut down during specific reorganizations. The fix covers 64-bit systems, but 32-bit systems and nodes using FAT32 storage remain affected. All three vulnerabilities were classified as easily discoverable through relatively simple methods, including large language model prompts. Project Loupe, led by Elias Rohrer at Spiral, identified the issues through automated AI scanning. Bitcoin Core's updated security disclosure policy accelerates publication when fixes are available for vulnerabilities considered easy to find. Combined with uncertainty following the Fed decision, the expiry gives traders another reason to monitor volatility closely. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Bitcoin Core bugs have emerged as BTC faces a fresh round of macroeconomic uncertainty. Developers disclosed three vulnerabilities on October 28, following AI-assisted security research by Project Loupe. The disclosures arrived just hours after the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady, leaving holders focused on Friday's $12 billion Bitcoin options expiry. The vulnerabilities affect Bitcoin Core, the software used by nodes to verify transactions and enforce Bitcoin's rules. One flaw could allow malicious peers to crash nodes running Windows, macOS, and BSD. Another could gradually exhaust memory, while a third could corrupt blockchain undo data under extreme conditions. Bitcoin Core developers have already released fixes across four maintained release branches. However, the timing puts network security alongside monetary policy and derivatives positioning in an unusually busy week. DISCOVER: 15+ Best Crypto IPO to Watch in 2026 The most serious of the three disclosed issues involves unbounded memory growth through TCP urgent data. A malicious peer could bypass normal memory protections and overwhelm vulnerable nodes running non-Linux operating systems. This flaw does not affect Linux nodes. A second vulnerability allows memory usage to grow gradually when a peer pretends to use an older Bitcoin protocol. The attacker can exploit weaknesses in message queuing and connection handling to keep accumulating data. Bitcoin Core estimates growth of up to 2 MB per hour per inbound peer and 5 MB per hour per outbound peer. The third issue concerns oversized undo files, which store information needed to disconnect blocks during reorganizations. Under extreme conditions, a miner could create valid blocks that push an undo file beyond 4 GB. The resulting corruption could cause affected nodes to shut down during specific reorganizations. The fix covers 64-bit systems, but 32-bit systems and nodes using FAT32 storage remain affected. All three vulnerabilities were classified as easily discoverable through relatively simple methods, including large language model prompts. The vulnerabilities affect Bitcoin Core, the software used by nodes to verify transactions and enforce Bitcoin's rules. One flaw could allow malicious peers to crash nodes running Windows, macOS, and BSD. The most serious of the three disclosed issues involves unbounded memory growth through TCP urgent data. A malicious peer could bypass normal memory protections and overwhelm vulnerable nodes running non-Linux operating systems. This flaw does not affect Linux nodes.

If they hold long positions, their trades could instead help limit the decline, Haeems said.US Regulators Allow Crypto Exchanges To Offer Stablecoin Rewards Despite Banks’ ConcernsWhy Could Volatility Rise After the Expiry?Options sellers who write contracts against their Bitcoin holdings typically sell new contracts as existing ones expire.

While many options are linked to prices well above current levels, contracts closer to Bitcoin’s market price could make dealer hedging activity important during the expiry.CoinMarketCap data showed Bitcoin at $79,861.75, down 1.11 per cent over 24 hours and 3.16 per cent over the past week at the time of writing.
If dealers are short options, their hedging activity could add to selling pressure if Bitcoin falls towards $75,000 to $78,000.

Adam Haeems, head of asset management at Tesseract Group, told Bloomberg that about 70 per cent of the expiring options’ gamma, a measure of how dealers’ hedging requirements change as prices move, is concentrated between $75,000 and $82,000.The direction of the impact will depend on dealers’ positions.
