extraction.body: Apple announced its first touchscreen laptop on October 28, 2026, and the price tag landed as loudly as the feature. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch, according to Ars Technica’s launch coverage . Both sizes use Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, and both go on sale November 6, 2026. For a company that spent more than a decade steering Mac owners toward the keyboard and trackpad, this is a real reversal. We tracked the build-up in our earlier look at the Pro and tell launch expectations , and the final product matches the broad outline. This analysis covers what Apple confirmed, what it left open, how the pricing compares with the rest of the market, and what the touchscreen MacBook Pro means for buyers, developers and rival laptop makers. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. It ships in two sizes, 14 inches and 16 inches. Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips power the lineup. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks. The headline feature is simple to state. You can now touch the Mac’s screen and expect it to respond. The harder question is what that changes in daily use. Apple has not turned the MacBook Pro into a tablet. The hardware stays a clamshell laptop with a keyboard and trackpad, and the touch layer sits on top of the existing Mac experience. How deeply macOS adapts to fingers, and which apps get touch-native controls on day one, remain open points that the announcement coverage does not settle. The Verge published the reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro , which gives the clearest first look at how Apple chose to present the change. CNN Business framed the news more bluntly, with a headline that called it Apple’s first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Reuters, Ars Technica and other outlets reached the same conclusion. The story is not that Apple copied a Windows feature. The story is that Apple moved at all. Three facts anchor everything else in this piece. First, the display technology is new to the MacBook Pro line. Second, the price floor sits well above where most people expect a laptop to start. Third, the on-sale date is only nine days away, so Apple has little time to let rumor fill the gaps. Those three facts shape the rest of the analysis below. The 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. The 16-inch starts at $3,399. The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price. Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence. BNN Bloomberg’s report on the first touchscreen laptops arriving amid a product blitz placed the launch inside a busy stretch for Apple, and that context matters for pricing. When a company launches several products in a short window, it usually prices the newest halo item high and lets cheaper models absorb the volume. A $2,899 entry point reads as a halo price, aimed at buyers who already pay for top-end Pro hardware. Pricing tells you who Apple expects to buy first. At these levels the customer is a working professional, a studio, or a company that buys machines in batches and writes them off. Casual users who want a touchscreen laptop for browsing and video calls have cheaper options on the Windows side. Apple appears comfortable ceding that segment for now. The panel is where the money goes. Apple’s reported specifications describe a tandem OLED display with up to 2,000 nits of brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. Tandem OLED stacks two emissive layers, which generally lets a panel reach higher brightness and last longer than a single-layer design. Apple has not, in the verified material, published lifetime or burn-in data for the new panel, so treat durability as an open question. Pairing a touch layer with OLED also creates engineering tradeoffs that Apple has not discussed in the verified coverage. Touch sensors, a protective surface and a glare-control finish all affect how a screen looks under bright light. Reviewers will test those tradeoffs once units reach them. Until then, the spec sheet tells you the ceiling and the review bench will tell you the reality. Apple chose its M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the new machines. We have no verified CPU or GPU core counts, memory ceilings, storage ceilings or battery-life numbers, so this section sticks to what is solid. The pairing signals that Apple sees the touchscreen MacBook Pro as a premium creative and engineering tool rather than a general-purpose entry laptop. Chip choice also frames the competition. Our own Apple Silicon vs Intel MacBook Pro comparison looked at how the M5 Max stacks up against Intel’s top mobile part, and the memory bandwidth gap was a central point. Apple’s advantage in efficiency per watt has shaped laptop buying for several years. Adding a touchscreen does not change that equation, but it does raise the question of what the new panel costs in battery life, a number Apple has not confirmed. The wider architecture story is covered in our ARM vs x86 analysis . The short version is that Apple’s unified memory design and its controlled software stack let it tune hardware and macOS together. That control becomes more important with touch, because input latency depends on the screen, the sensor, the chip and the operating system acting as one pipeline. Windows laptop makers assemble that pipeline from parts supplied by many companies. Apple builds it in house. Coverage names John Ternus as the Apple executive who unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks, and identifies him as the company’s CEO. His role in the presentation carries weight. Putting the chief executive on stage for a hardware reversal this large sends a message about how much weight Apple places on the change. The event name, “Pro and tell,” also hints at the framing. The name points to a professional-first pitch. That fits the pricing and the chip selection, and it fits the way Apple has historically introduced new display technology on its highest-priced models before spreading it down the range. Past launches, from the first Retina MacBook Pro to the mini-LED displays, followed a similar path. Apple did experiment. In 2016 it added the Touch Bar, a thin touch strip above the keyboard on some MacBook Pro models, as a way to bring touch to the Mac without touching the main screen. The idea never became a staple of daily use for most owners, and Apple dropped it from the redesigned Pro line in 2021. The episode showed Apple was willing to try touch but unwilling to put it on the display itself. For years the iPad served as Apple’s answer to anyone who wanted touch with serious software. Add a keyboard case and the tablet behaves like a small laptop. That strategy kept the product lines distinct, with the Mac for desktop-class work and the iPad for touch. The new MacBook Pro blurs the line. Our coverage of the iPad mini’s move to OLED shows Apple pushing OLED across touch devices at the same time, which suggests a broader display strategy rather than a one-off experiment. CNN’s report on the first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen underlines how much the company’s position has shifted. Whatever Apple’s internal reasoning, the market pressure is plain. Buyers who use pen input, tablets and phones all day increasingly expect a screen to respond to a tap. Apple appears to have decided that holding out cost more than conceding. The gaps in the announcement are as useful to know as the specs. Several details that buyers will want before spending $2,899 or more are not in the verified record. We list them here so readers do not mistake rumor for fact. Battery life deserves special attention. OLED panels draw different power than LCD panels depending on what is on screen, and a touch layer adds its own overhead. Apple’s claims will matter, and independent testing will matter more. If you plan to buy on November 6, wait for reviews that run the same workload on the old and new models. Repair cost is another unknown. OLED screens cost more to replace than LCD panels, and a touch OLED sits in a more exposed position because people will now press on it. Our report on Apple replacing iPhone Duo inner displays covers a $999 fix, and while that product differs, it shows how steep a premium display repair can run. No verified source has yet given a screen repair price for the touchscreen MacBook Pro. Apple enters a market that has long offered touch. Windows makers from Lenovo to Dell to HP ship touchscreen laptops at nearly every price point, and many of them flip into tablet modes. Apple’s entry is narrower. It sells one family at the high end and does not offer a convertible hinge in the verified details. That makes the comparison less about features and more about philosophy. The table highlights Apple’s strategic bet. It does not compete on price. It competes on display quality, chip efficiency and software integration. If those advantages show up in testing, buyers who value them will accept the premium. If they do not, Windows rivals with lower prices and years of touch refinement will pitch themselves as the smarter value. TechCrunch’s write-up of Apple launching its new touchscreen MacBook Pro reported the release as a product launch, and the market read-through follows from that. Component suppliers that make OLED panels and touch sensors for large laptop screens gain a major volume customer if Apple scales production. Rival laptop makers lose one of their long-standing talking points, because a touchscreen no longer separates a Windows machine from a Mac. Retailers and resellers face a trickier picture. Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. It ships in two sizes, 14 inches and 16 inches. Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips power the lineup. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks.

The headline feature is simple to state. You can now touch the Mac’s screen and expect it to respond. The harder question is what that changes in daily use. Apple has not turned the MacBook Pro into a tablet. The hardware stays a clamshell laptop with a keyboard and trackpad, and the touch layer sits on top of the existing Mac experience. How deeply macOS adapts to fingers, and which apps get touch-native controls on day one, remain open points that the announcement coverage does not settle.

The Verge published the reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro , which gives the clearest first look at how Apple chose to present the change. CNN Business framed the news more bluntly, with a headline that called it Apple’s first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Reuters, Ars Technica and other outlets reached the same conclusion. The story is not that Apple copied a Windows feature. The story is that Apple moved at all.

Three facts anchor everything else in this piece. First, the display technology is new to the MacBook Pro line. Second, the price floor sits well above where most people expect a laptop to start. Third, the on-sale date is only nine days away, so Apple has little time to let rumor fill the gaps. Those three facts shape the rest of the analysis below.

The 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. The 16-inch starts at $3,399. The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price. Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence.

BNN Bloomberg’s report on the first touchscreen laptops arriving amid a product blitz placed the launch inside a busy stretch for Apple, and that context matters for pricing. When a company launches several products in a short window, it usually prices the newest halo item high and lets cheaper models absorb the volume. A $2,899 entry point reads as a halo price, aimed at buyers who already pay for top-end Pro hardware.

Pricing tells you who Apple expects to buy first. At these levels the customer is a working professional, a studio, or a company that buys machines in batches and writes them off. Casual users who want a touchscreen laptop for browsing and video calls have cheaper options on the Windows side. Apple appears comfortable ceding that segment for now.

The panel is where the money goes. Apple’s reported specifications describe a tandem OLED display with up to 2,000 nits of brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. Tandem OLED stacks two emissive layers, which generally lets a panel reach higher brightness and last longer than a single-layer design. Apple has not, in the verified material, published lifetime or burn-in data for the new panel, so treat durability as an open question.

Pairing a touch layer with OLED also creates engineering tradeoffs that Apple has not discussed in the verified coverage. Touch sensors, a protective surface and a glare-control finish all affect how a screen looks under bright light. Reviewers will test those tradeoffs once units reach them. Until then, the spec sheet tells you the ceiling and the review bench will tell you the reality.

Apple chose its M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the new machines. We have no verified CPU or GPU core counts, memory ceilings, storage ceilings or battery-life numbers, so this section sticks to what is solid. The pairing signals that Apple sees the touchscreen MacBook Pro as a premium creative and engineering tool rather than a general-purpose entry laptop.

Chip choice also frames the competition. Our own Apple Silicon vs Intel MacBook Pro comparison looked at how the M5 Max stacks up against Intel’s top mobile part, and the memory bandwidth gap was a central point. Apple’s advantage in efficiency per watt has shaped laptop buying for several years. Adding a touchscreen does not change that equation, but it does raise the question of what the new panel costs in battery life, a number Apple has not confirmed.

The wider architecture story is covered in our ARM vs x86 analysis . The short version is that Apple’s unified memory design and its controlled software stack let it tune hardware and macOS together. That control becomes more important with touch, because input latency depends on the screen, the sensor, the chip and the operating system acting as one pipeline. Windows laptop makers assemble that pipeline from parts supplied by many companies. Apple builds it in house.

Putting the chief executive on stage for a hardware reversal this large sends a message about how much weight Apple places on the change.

The event name, “Pro and tell,” also hints at the framing. The name points to a professional-first pitch. That fits the pricing and the chip selection, and it fits the way Apple has historically introduced new display technology on its highest-priced models before spreading it down the range. Past launches, from the first Retina MacBook Pro to the mini-LED displays, followed a similar path.

CNN’s report on the first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen underlines how much the company’s position has shifted. Whatever Apple’s internal reasoning, the market pressure is plain. Buyers who use pen input, tablets and phones all day increasingly expect a screen to respond to a tap. Apple appears to have decided that holding out cost more than conceding.

Apple’s claims will matter, and independent testing will matter more. If you plan to buy on November 6, wait for reviews that run the same workload on the old and new models.

Repair cost is another unknown. OLED screens cost more to replace than LCD panels, and a touch OLED sits in a more exposed position because people will now press on it. Our report on Apple replacing iPhone Duo inner displays covers a $999 fix, and while that product differs, it shows how steep a premium display repair can run. No verified source has yet given a screen repair price for the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

extraction.body: Commentary: Yes, I’m judgy about how smudgy Apple’s new laptop screen is going to be. I had to suppress a shudder at the thought of how smudgy the touchscreen display on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is going to get. Unlike every other Apple laptop, you can directly tap and swipe on this new MacBook Pro screen like an iPad or iPhone. I try to rarely even brush the screen of my laptop, and yet it still ends up with its share of oily smudges. To be clear: It’s not like I’m reaching into a bucket of greasy fried chicken when typing away at my MacBook Pro. But even with normal use, skin oils build up on the keyboard. Shutting the laptop brings those oily keys directly into contact with the glass, stamping the display with a ghostly grid of gunk. Ages ago, I would slip a microfiber cloth between the screen and keyboard whenever I shut my laptop, but I eventually gave that up. Now, I regularly wipe it down with a screen-cleaning spray called Whoosh, recommended to me by an Apple Store employee. The new MacBook Pro gets the same oleophobic coating, a surface treatment meant to minimize fingerprints, as found on iPad, iPhone and the announced HomeView . We’ll have to see if it’s any more or less successful on the large PROLED XDR display when we test it out. The least Apple could have done was include its $9 Polishing Cloth for free, but the cloth remains a separate accessory purchase. A touchscreen Apple laptop has been inevitable since the first iPad — heck, even the first iPhone — which has trained a generation that screens are meant to be tapped, swiped and pinched. Apple even tested a laptop touch interface with the Touch Bar on MacBook Pros for several years before finally giving up. People I love and respect nonetheless send a shiver down my spine when they stab their laptop screen — or worse, touch my screen — to point out something. I’ll take the MacBook Pro’s Touch Bar over a touch screen. Am I oversensitive to fingerprints on a screen? Most definitely. But I know I’m not the only one. As a photographer, I want to see my photos on the best possible screen, and this one is certainly Apple’s premium laptop display. Because it’s OLED, the blacks should be truly black, and colors look extremely vibrant. Apple says its 2,000-nit brightness makes it easy to use in bright light, and it has a wider color gamut that covers both P3 and Adobe RGB color spaces. But I also want to know that when I’m using software to remove errant dust spots from my images, I’m not clicking the same area four times because the spot is actually a smudge on the glass. Could I buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR and never touch the screen? Probably. But that feels like paying extra for a feature I wouldn’t use, even though the improvements are rolled in. You can’t get the OLED quality without the touchscreen. And making it a touchscreen display invites more skin-to-glass contact. The question is whether I’d be able to keep my paws off the screen when I just want to zoom in on a map or dismiss a notification. For the time being, a touchscreen Mac isn’t high on my list of features. But as I type this, I am realizing my display is once again in serious need of a good cleaning. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

passages: The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs.
Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips.
Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen.
Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers.
Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO.
“Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event.

extraction.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price.
Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence.

extraction.body: Commentary: Yes, I’m judgy about how smudgy Apple’s new laptop screen is going to be. I had to suppress a shudder at the thought of how smudgy the touchscreen display on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is going to get. Unlike every other Apple laptop, you can directly tap and swipe on this new MacBook Pro screen like an iPad or iPhone. I try to rarely even brush the screen of my laptop, and yet it still ends up with its share of oily smudges. To be clear: It’s not like I’m reaching into a bucket of greasy fried chicken when typing away at my MacBook Pro. But even with normal use, skin oils build up on the keyboard. Shutting the laptop brings those oily keys directly into contact with the glass, stamping the display with a ghostly grid of gunk. Ages ago, I would slip a microfiber cloth between the screen and keyboard whenever I shut my laptop, but I eventually gave that up. Now, I regularly wipe it down with a screen-cleaning spray called Whoosh, recommended to me by an Apple Store employee. The new MacBook Pro gets the same oleophobic coating, a surface treatment meant to minimize fingerprints, as found on iPad, iPhone and the announced HomeView . We’ll have to see if it’s any more or less successful on the large PROLED XDR display when we test it out. The least Apple could have done was include its $9 Polishing Cloth for free, but the cloth remains a separate accessory purchase. A touchscreen Apple laptop has been inevitable since the first iPad — heck, even the first iPhone — which has trained a generation that screens are meant to be tapped, swiped and pinched. Apple even tested a laptop touch interface with the Touch Bar on MacBook Pros for several years before finally giving up. People I love and respect nonetheless send a shiver down my spine when they stab their laptop screen — or worse, touch my screen — to point out something. I’ll take the MacBook Pro’s Touch Bar over a touch screen. Am I oversensitive to fingerprints on a screen? Most definitely. But I know I’m not the only one. As a photographer, I want to see my photos on the best possible screen, and this one is certainly Apple’s premium laptop display. Because it’s OLED, the blacks should be truly black, and colors look extremely vibrant. Apple says its 2,000-nit brightness makes it easy to use in bright light, and it has a wider color gamut that covers both P3 and Adobe RGB color spaces. But I also want to know that when I’m using software to remove errant dust spots from my images, I’m not clicking the same area four times because the spot is actually a smudge on the glass. Could I buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR and never touch the screen? Probably. But that feels like paying extra for a feature I wouldn’t use, even though the improvements are rolled in. You can’t get the OLED quality without the touchscreen. And making it a touchscreen display invites more skin-to-glass contact. The question is whether I’d be able to keep my paws off the screen when I just want to zoom in on a map or dismiss a notification. For the time being, a touchscreen Mac isn’t high on my list of features. But as I type this, I am realizing my display is once again in serious need of a good cleaning. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

sources.title: Apple just announced its first ever MacBook with a touchscreen
passages: The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs.
Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips.
Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen.
Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers.
Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO.
“Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event.
Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work.
Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise.
Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

extraction.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

extraction.body: Legislation introduced by U.S. Rep. Rich McCormick would advance cybersecurity standards at a critical inflection point for AI and cloud security WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aviatrix® welcomes the introduction of the Common-Sense Cloud Security Act by U.S. Rep. Rich McCormick today. The legislation would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated cybersecurity standards, methodologies, and recommendations for cloud-based infrastructure at a critical inflection point for AI and cloud security. "The Common-Sense Cloud Security Act is an important step toward aligning federal cybersecurity standards with the cloud environments that now support government systems, critical infrastructure, and the modern enterprise," said Doug Merritt, CEO and Chairman of Aviatrix. "Cloud security can no longer be treated as a perimeter problem. We are in the Containment Era, a fundamental shift in how organizations must think about securing cloud environments, and this legislation recognizes that reality." The company supports the legislation as an advocate for modernized cloud security standards and stronger public-private collaboration at a time when the cloud has become central to national security, economic resilience, and the delivery of critical services. Enterprise cloud migration across the public and private sectors has delivered speed, scale and efficiency, but security standards have not always modernized at the same pace. Existing cybersecurity programs remain essential, but many still rely heavily on approaches designed for data-center-era environments. The cloud's scale, complexity and interconnected nature require standards that account for activity inside cloud environments, not only at the perimeter. The rapid adoption of AI workloads is intensifying this challenge, and the frontier models in use today have already demonstrated significant offensive capability. AI agents and workloads are multiplying faster than security teams can review them, and every one of them inherits the access paths of the infrastructure it runs on. These workloads are often ephemeral enough to evade traditional agent-based controls, privileged enough to concentrate risk, and deployed fast enough to outrun manual review. As enterprises scale AI across cloud environments, the Blast Radius of a single compromised workload or misused agent grows with every path it inherits. The Common-Sense Cloud Security Act would help address that gap by encouraging standards that can evolve alongside modern cloud architectures and emerging AI-driven cyber threats. Aviatrix believes industry and government must continue working together to promote consistent, modern cloud security practices across public-sector systems, critical infrastructure and private enterprise. "In the Containment Era, organizations need standards that recognize how modern attacks move through legitimate credentials, trusted systems and ungoverned communication paths inside complex cloud environments," Merritt added. "The question is no longer whether AI will reshape the enterprise; it's whether security architecture can keep pace. Aviatrix is proud to support this legislation and the broader public-private effort to strengthen cloud security as cyber threats continue to proliferate." We are in the Containment Era, a fundamental shift in how organizations must think about securing cloud environments, and this legislation recognizes that reality."

The company supports the legislation as an advocate for modernized cloud security standards and stronger public-private collaboration at a time when the cloud has become central to national security, economic resilience, and the delivery of critical services.

Enterprise cloud migration across the public and private sectors has delivered speed, scale and efficiency, but security standards have not always modernized at the same pace. Existing cybersecurity programs remain essential, but many still rely heavily on approaches designed for data-center-era environments. The cloud's scale, complexity and interconnected nature require standards that account for activity inside cloud environments, not only at the perimeter.

The rapid adoption of AI workloads is intensifying this challenge, and the frontier models in use today have already demonstrated significant offensive capability. As enterprises scale AI across cloud environments, the Blast Radius of a single compromised workload or misused agent grows with every path it inherits.

extraction.body: A bipartisan proposal directs NIST to create updated cybersecurity frameworks, AI threat detection tools and a voluntary cloud certification program. Federal standards for cloud computing infrastructure would see substantial updates under legislation introduced by U.S. Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., aimed at shielding sensitive data and essential utility networks from sophisticated cyber intrusions. The Common-Sense Cloud Security Act directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to establish modernized cybersecurity protocols for cloud environments. Under the proposal, NIST would collaborate with federal cybersecurity agencies, industry cloud service providers, academic researchers and critical infrastructure operators to address architectural vulnerabilities. The bill outlines a framework for deploying artificial intelligence systems to detect anomalies and identify unauthorized network behavior. It also directs NIST to formulate frameworks for digital identity protection that link account credentials directly to designated physical hardware to prevent remote credential hijacking. To assist commercial adoption, the legislation establishes a tiered, voluntary Cloud Security Certification Program. Under this system, independent accredited laboratories would evaluate and certify that commercial providers meet baseline federal criteria. The measure also targets supply-chain risks by mandating procedures for vetting, authorizing and monitoring third-party software integrations connected to core cloud platforms. In addition, the legislation requires updates to the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program to align federal procurement with revised baseline standards. NIST would also be required to build a standardized breach-assessment methodology to measure how far an intrusion could spread across interconnected networks, alongside recurring reporting requirements to Congress detailing private-sector compliance barriers. Jesse Jacobs is assistant editor of SecurityToday.com . extraction.body: Legislation introduced by U.S. Rep. Rich McCormick would advance cybersecurity standards at a critical inflection point for AI and cloud security WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aviatrix® welcomes the introduction of the Common-Sense Cloud Security Act by U.S. Rep. Rich McCormick today. The legislation would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated cybersecurity standards, methodologies, and recommendations for cloud-based infrastructure at a critical inflection point for AI and cloud security. "The Common-Sense Cloud Security Act is an important step toward aligning federal cybersecurity standards with the cloud environments that now support government systems, critical infrastructure, and the modern enterprise," said Doug Merritt, CEO and Chairman of Aviatrix. "Cloud security can no longer be treated as a perimeter problem. We are in the Containment Era, a fundamental shift in how organizations must think about securing cloud environments, and this legislation recognizes that reality." The company supports the legislation as an advocate for modernized cloud security standards and stronger public-private collaboration at a time when the cloud has become central to national security, economic resilience, and the delivery of critical services. Enterprise cloud migration across the public and private sectors has delivered speed, scale and efficiency, but security standards have not always modernized at the same pace. Existing cybersecurity programs remain essential, but many still rely heavily on approaches designed for data-center-era environments. The cloud's scale, complexity and interconnected nature require standards that account for activity inside cloud environments, not only at the perimeter. The rapid adoption of AI workloads is intensifying this challenge, and the frontier models in use today have already demonstrated significant offensive capability. AI agents and workloads are multiplying faster than security teams can review them, and every one of them inherits the access paths of the infrastructure it runs on. These workloads are often ephemeral enough to evade traditional agent-based controls, privileged enough to concentrate risk, and deployed fast enough to outrun manual review. As enterprises scale AI across cloud environments, the Blast Radius of a single compromised workload or misused agent grows with every path it inherits. The Common-Sense Cloud Security Act would help address that gap by encouraging standards that can evolve alongside modern cloud architectures and emerging AI-driven cyber threats. Aviatrix believes industry and government must continue working together to promote consistent, modern cloud security practices across public-sector systems, critical infrastructure and private enterprise. "In the Containment Era, organizations need standards that recognize how modern attacks move through legitimate credentials, trusted systems and ungoverned communication paths inside complex cloud environments," Merritt added. "The question is no longer whether AI will reshape the enterprise; it's whether security architecture can keep pace. Aviatrix is proud to support this legislation and the broader public-private effort to strengthen cloud security as cyber threats continue to proliferate." Aviatrix defines the Containment Era as a fundamental shift in cybersecurity, where the primary challenge has moved from keeping attackers out to limiting what they can reach once inside. In the Containment Era, containment is the architectural enforcement of explicit communication policy at every workload — governing what it can reach and what can reach it, at the granularity of workload identity and protocol — on every path available to it, independent of whether a compromise has been detected. Aviatrix put that standard into practice on October 26 with the launch of Aviatrix Clearance , a new offering on the Aviatrix Containment Platform, built on the Cloud Native Security Fabric. Clearance lets security teams limit each cloud workload to the paths it needs, outbound and lateral, and enforce that policy safely: each policy runs in monitor mode first, shows what it would block before it blocks anything, and backs out in one action. Through its Clearance Incident Response Program , Aviatrix is making Clearance free for every enterprise across its entire estate from November 1, 2026, through May 1, 2027. This gives security teams time to patch with a containment backstop in place. About Aviatrix Aviatrix® is the network containment company. The Aviatrix Containment Platform sets what every cloud workload may reach before any attack, so a compromised workload does not become a company-wide breach. Built on the Cloud Native Security Fabric, it enforces that policy in the network, at every workload and in every cloud, with nothing to install and nothing to detect first, and encrypts the traffic it allows. It is simpler, safer, faster, and less costly than the firewalls and agents it replaces. The Cloud Native Security Fabric is quantum safe. Trusted by more than 500 of the world's leading enterprises. For more information, visit aviatrix.ai.

extraction.body: A bipartisan proposal directs NIST to create updated cybersecurity frameworks, AI threat detection tools and a voluntary cloud certification program. Federal standards for cloud computing infrastructure would see substantial updates under legislation introduced by U.S. Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., aimed at shielding sensitive data and essential utility networks from sophisticated cyber intrusions. The Common-Sense Cloud Security Act directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to establish modernized cybersecurity protocols for cloud environments. Under the proposal, NIST would collaborate with federal cybersecurity agencies, industry cloud service providers, academic researchers and critical infrastructure operators to address architectural vulnerabilities. The bill outlines a framework for deploying artificial intelligence systems to detect anomalies and identify unauthorized network behavior. It also directs NIST to formulate frameworks for digital identity protection that link account credentials directly to designated physical hardware to prevent remote credential hijacking. To assist commercial adoption, the legislation establishes a tiered, voluntary Cloud Security Certification Program. Under this system, independent accredited laboratories would evaluate and certify that commercial providers meet baseline federal criteria. The measure also targets supply-chain risks by mandating procedures for vetting, authorizing and monitoring third-party software integrations connected to core cloud platforms. In addition, the legislation requires updates to the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program to align federal procurement with revised baseline standards. NIST would also be required to build a standardized breach-assessment methodology to measure how far an intrusion could spread across interconnected networks, alongside recurring reporting requirements to Congress detailing private-sector compliance barriers. Jesse Jacobs is assistant editor of SecurityToday.com . sources.title: Trump orders cuts to South Korea joint drills despite warnings about Kim regime | North Korea - The Guardian
passages: Donald Trump has said he is scaling back joint US military drills with South Korea aimed at deterring North Korea, despite military officials from both countries warning that Kim Jong-un’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from the Ukraine war.
Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them.
He also said South Korea had refused to help in the “denuclearisation of the Islamic republic of Iran”.

South Korea’s presidential Blue House said it was reviewing Trump’s post and “hopes that the friendly relationship between the US and North Korean leaders will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two ⁠countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean peninsula”.
Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, added that Pyongyang was unlikely to be moved by Trump’s announcement.
“The North will only view it as meaningful if the joint exercises are cancelled in their entirety rather than scaled back.
It has little reason to see this as meaningful.”

Speaking to the Guardian at a separate briefing, Lt Gen Scott Winter, deputy commander of the UNC, said the threats being countered “reflect the increased use of these technologies and the understanding that North Korea has contemporary battlefield experience”.
Trump has previously suspended major US-South Korean military exercises in pursuit of diplomacy with Kim.
The exercises were subsequently redesigned and resumed in modified forms and names.

He said the US-South Korea alliance remained “extremely important” but argued that Seoul should gradually reduce its security dependence on Washington and move towards securing its own nuclear arms, an idea that has broad public support in South Korea despite being rejected by the government and opposed internationally.
“The cost savings from downsizing drills are marginal, while the diplomatic benefits for relations with North Korea are doubtful,” he told Agence France-Presse.
“This is a very serious improvement in North Korean capabilities.
And we should not take lightly this threat environment.”

North Korea has deepened military ties with Russia since the two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership pact in June 2024, seeing Pyongyang provide troops, artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to support Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
“They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea, that changes the DPRK capability,” Donald said, referring to North Korea’s formal name.
In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details.

However, Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, cautioned that downsizing the exercise would “slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defence, and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia”.
He added that they were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”.

More than 14,000 North Korean troops have fought alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region, and Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 more.

The allies would continue coordinating on their combined defence posture and military exercises, it said. In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details. “I understand him,” the president said. “He understands me.” Over the weekend, Trump also shared an old photo of him posing with the North Korean leader on Truth Social, repeating his claim the two “get along great”, leading to speculation he would renew his attempt to have a summit with Kim. After his first summit with the North Korean leader in 2018, that year’s Ulchi Freedom Guardian exercise was cancelled , while other drills were suspended or scaled back. The exercises were subsequently redesigned and resumed in modified forms and names. Cheong Seong-chang, the vice-president of the Seoul-based Sejong Institute thinktank, said Trump could go further if he meets Kim again, potentially deciding to suspend the exercises altogether or reduce US troop levels without consulting South Korea. He said the US-South Korea alliance remained “extremely important” but argued that Seoul should gradually reduce its security dependence on Washington and move towards securing its own nuclear arms, an idea that has broad public support in South Korea despite being rejected by the government and opposed internationally. However, Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, cautioned that downsizing the exercise would “slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defence, and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia”. “The cost savings from downsizing drills are marginal, while the diplomatic benefits for relations with North Korea are doubtful,” he told Agence France-Presse. Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, added that Pyongyang was unlikely to be moved by Trump’s announcement. “The North will only view it as meaningful if the joint exercises are cancelled in their entirety rather than scaled back. It has little reason to see this as meaningful.” Last week, South Korean and US military officials said they would incorporate into the drills lessons drawn from North Korean troops’ increasing battlefield experience in Ukraine , including new drone tactics. North Korea has deepened military ties with Russia since the two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership pact in June 2024, seeing Pyongyang provide troops, artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to support Moscow’s war in Ukraine. At a joint briefing, Col Ryan Donald, the public affairs director for the US-led commands in South Korea, said this year’s scenario would reflect “drones, GPS disruption [and] cyber-attacks”, threats he linked directly to North Korean soldiers who have deployed and fought in Ukraine as part of Pyongyang’s military support for Russia. “They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea, that changes the DPRK capability,” Donald said, referring to North Korea’s formal name. “Our training accounts for that threat, that is why the exercise looks different [from previous exercises], and over the last five years it’s continually evolved.” Speaking to the Guardian at a separate briefing, Lt Gen Scott Winter, deputy commander of the UNC, said the threats being countered “reflect the increased use of these technologies and the understanding that North Korea has contemporary battlefield experience”. “We’re very conscious that North Korea has used this as an opportunity to test a number of its ballistic missile systems,” he said, adding that this year’s drills would be “bigger and better than ever”. More than 14,000 North Korean troops have fought alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region, and Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 more. The two countries are also close to completing the first road bridge ever built between them, over the Tumen river, which one open-source investigation concluded functions more as a military logistics corridor than a trade route. Russian state media says it is expected to open in September. In the days before the exercise were due to begin, North Korea test-fired ballistic missiles, in what analysts read partly as a protest against the drills. On Friday, North Korea’s foreign ministry called the exercise “a rehearsal for an aggressive war”, warning it would “respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent”. The warning is typical of the rhetoric Pyongyang deploys ahead of major US-South Korean drills. Officials have repeatedly described the exercise as “defensive” in nature. Chun In-bum, a retired lieutenant general who commanded South Korea’s special forces, highlighted the importance of preparing in a timely manner for capabilities that will be required to prepare for new challenges ahead. “This is a very serious improvement in North Korean capabilities. And we should not take lightly this threat environment.”

However, on Sunday evening, Trump said he was “not happy” with US participation “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”. He added that they were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”.

Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them. He also said South Korea had refused to help in the “denuclearisation of the Islamic republic of Iran”.

South Korea’s presidential Blue House said it was reviewing Trump’s post and “hopes that the friendly relationship between the US and North Korean leaders will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two ⁠countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean peninsula”.
The allies would continue coordinating on their combined defence posture and military exercises, it said.
In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details. “I understand him,” the president said. “He understands me.”

Over the weekend, Trump also shared an old photo of him posing with the North Korean leader on Truth Social, repeating his claim the two “get along great”, leading to speculation he would renew his attempt to have a summit with Kim.

Trump has previously suspended major US-South Korean military exercises in pursuit of diplomacy with Kim. He said the US-South Korea alliance remained “extremely important” but argued that Seoul should gradually reduce its security dependence on Washington and move towards securing its own nuclear arms, an idea that has broad public support in South Korea despite being rejected by the government and opposed internationally.

However, Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, cautioned that downsizing the exercise would “slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defence, and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia”.
“The cost savings from downsizing drills are marginal, while the diplomatic benefits for relations with North Korea are doubtful,” he told Agence France-Presse.

Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, added that Pyongyang was unlikely to be moved by Trump’s announcement. “The North will only view it as meaningful if the joint exercises are cancelled in their entirety rather than scaled back. passages: SEOUL, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Germany and South Korea set out an enhanced security partnership on Thursday, arguing that growing cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang showed that European and Asian security were increasingly intertwined.

Since 2024, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to fight alongside Russians, as well as weapons to replenish Moscow's dwindling armoury, while gaining valuable battlefield experience, South Korea's intelligence agency has said.
"Korean defence companies have great interest in long-term partnerships with Germany, including joint ventures and joint development projects," Lee said.
South Korea is the final stop on Merz's week-long trip to Asia, which has also taken him to Singapore and Japan.

At a summit in Seoul the two governments agreed to expand cooperation in defence and security, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said, adding that they planned to conclude an agreement on the protection of classified military information.

passages: Yonhap Russian President Vladimir Putin was set to make his first visit to North Korea in 24 years Tuesday for talks with leader Kim Jong-un in a highly symbolic trip showing off their ever-tightening relations amid deepening concerns about military cooperation.

Reuters-Yonhap Experts said Putin's trip will likely pave the way for deeper military cooperation between the two nations beyond arms transactions at a time when North Korea and Russia are voicing their solidarity against the United States.

Analysts said Kim and Putin may adopt a joint declaration that calls for both sides to elevate the level of military, security and economic cooperation but saw a low possibility of them clinching a treaty akin to a military alliance.

Putin will arrive in Pyongyang on Tuesday evening and sign "important" documents with the North's leader Wednesday, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as telling reporters by Russia's news agency TASS.
But the deal was scrapped in 1996 after the Soviet Union established diplomatic ties with South Korea in 1990 and collapsed the following year.
It also comes nine months after Kim traveled to Russia's Far East in September last year for a summit with Putin.
In late May, North Korea's attempt to launch a military spy satellite ended in failure as a satellite-carrying rocket exploded right after liftoff.

extraction.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, second from left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, meet at Russia's Vostochny spaceport in this picture provided by the North's official Korean Central News Agency, Sept. Yonhap Russian President Vladimir Putin was set to make his first visit to North Korea in 24 years Tuesday for talks with leader Kim Jong-un in a highly symbolic trip showing off their ever-tightening relations amid deepening concerns about military cooperation. Putin will "pay a state visit" to North Korea for a two-day trip at the invitation of the North's leader, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported in a one-sentence dispatch Monday. It will mark Putin's first trip to North Korea since July 2000, when he met with former North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, the late father of the current leader. It also comes nine months after Kim traveled to Russia's Far East in September last year for a summit with Putin. Since then, the two nations have been bolstering military ties and expanding the scope of cooperation in various fields, with the North supplying Russia with ammunition for its war in Ukraine in exchange for aid and suspected technological assistance for its space program. Putin will arrive in Pyongyang on Tuesday evening and sign "important" documents with the North's leader Wednesday, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as telling reporters by Russia's news agency TASS. "Several documents will be signed ... and this can be said about a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty," Ushakov said, adding that if it is signed, it would "outline prospects for further cooperation" between the two nations. Russian President Vladimir Putin watches honor guards pass by during a flower-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Victory Day, which marks the 79th anniversary of the victory over Nazi Germany in World War Two, in central Moscow, Russia, May 9. Reuters-Yonhap Experts said Putin's trip will likely pave the way for deeper military cooperation between the two nations beyond arms transactions at a time when North Korea and Russia are voicing their solidarity against the United States. Pyongyang is accused of providing weapons and munitions to Russia for use in Moscow's war in Ukraine in return for Russia's suspected technical assistance in the development of North Korea's spy satellite program and economic assistance. Analysts said Kim and Putin may adopt a joint declaration that calls for both sides to elevate the level of military, security and economic cooperation but saw a low possibility of them clinching a treaty akin to a military alliance. North Korea and the former Soviet Union signed a treaty of friendship and mutual assistance in 1961, when the North's national founder Kim Il-sung visited Moscow. The treaty included a provision for the so-called automatic military intervention, under which if one side is under an armed attack, the other provides military troops and other aid without hesitation. But the deal was scrapped in 1996 after the Soviet Union established diplomatic ties with South Korea in 1990 and collapsed the following year. In 2000, North Korea and Russia signed a new treaty of bilateral cooperation, but it did not contain such a provision, though it stated that both sides "immediately make contacts" in case one of them faces a crisis of being invaded. Experts said North Korea and Russia are expected to highlight cooperation in the economic sector, as their arms deals and military cooperation constitute a violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions banning Pyongyang's nuclear and missile programs. coreStoryFacts.text: Donald Trump has said he is scaling back joint US military drills with South Korea aimed at deterring North Korea, despite military officials from both countries warning that Kim Jong-un’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from the Ukraine war.
Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them.
He also said South Korea had refused to help in the “denuclearisation of the Islamic republic of Iran”.

South Korea’s presidential Blue House said it was reviewing Trump’s post and “hopes that the friendly relationship between the US and North Korean leaders will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two ⁠countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean peninsula”.
Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, added that Pyongyang was unlikely to be moved by Trump’s announcement.
“The North will only view it as meaningful if the joint exercises are cancelled in their entirety rather than scaled back.
It has little reason to see this as meaningful.”

Speaking to the Guardian at a separate briefing, Lt Gen Scott Winter, deputy commander of the UNC, said the threats being countered “reflect the increased use of these technologies and the understanding that North Korea has contemporary battlefield experience”.
Trump has previously suspended major US-South Korean military exercises in pursuit of diplomacy with Kim.
The exercises were subsequently redesigned and resumed in modified forms and names.

He said the US-South Korea alliance remained “extremely important” but argued that Seoul should gradually reduce its security dependence on Washington and move towards securing its own nuclear arms, an idea that has broad public support in South Korea despite being rejected by the government and opposed internationally.
“The cost savings from downsizing drills are marginal, while the diplomatic benefits for relations with North Korea are doubtful,” he told Agence France-Presse.
“This is a very serious improvement in North Korean capabilities.
And we should not take lightly this threat environment.”

North Korea has deepened military ties with Russia since the two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership pact in June 2024, seeing Pyongyang provide troops, artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to support Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
“They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea, that changes the DPRK capability,” Donald said, referring to North Korea’s formal name.
In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details.

However, Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, cautioned that downsizing the exercise would “slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defence, and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia”.
He added that they were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”.

More than 14,000 North Korean troops have fought alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region, and Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 more.

SEOUL, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Germany and South Korea set out an enhanced security partnership on Thursday, arguing that growing cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang showed that European and Asian security were increasingly intertwined.

Since 2024, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to fight alongside Russians, as well as weapons to replenish Moscow's dwindling armoury, while gaining valuable battlefield experience, South Korea's intelligence agency has said.
"Korean defence companies have great interest in long-term partnerships with Germany, including joint ventures and joint development projects," Lee said.
South Korea is the final stop on Merz's week-long trip to Asia, which has also taken him to Singapore and Japan.

Donald Trump has said he is scaling back joint US military drills with South Korea aimed at deterring North Korea, despite military officials from both countries warning that Kim Jong-un’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from the Ukraine war.
The drills under Ulchi Freedom Shield, one of two main annual exercises held by South Korea and the US, start on Monday and run until 27 August.

They were expected to involve about 18,000 South Korean troops, alongside US forces and personnel from 11 of the 18 member states of the United Nations Command (UNC), the multinational body that oversees the 1953 armistice that halted hostilities of the Korean war.

However, on Sunday evening, Trump said he was “not happy” with US participation “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”. He added that they were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”.

Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them. He also said South Korea had refused to help in the “denuclearisation of the Islamic republic of Iran”.

South Korea’s presidential Blue House said it was reviewing Trump’s post and “hopes that the friendly relationship between the US and North Korean leaders will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two ⁠countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean peninsula”.
The allies would continue coordinating on their combined defence posture and military exercises, it said.
In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details. “I understand him,” the president said. “He understands me.”

However, Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, cautioned that downsizing the exercise would “slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defence, and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia”.

sources.title: Putin set to arrive in N. Korea in rare trip amid deepening concerns about military cooperation
passages: Yonhap Russian President Vladimir Putin was set to make his first visit to North Korea in 24 years Tuesday for talks with leader Kim Jong-un in a highly symbolic trip showing off their ever-tightening relations amid deepening concerns about military cooperation.

Reuters-Yonhap Experts said Putin's trip will likely pave the way for deeper military cooperation between the two nations beyond arms transactions at a time when North Korea and Russia are voicing their solidarity against the United States.

Analysts said Kim and Putin may adopt a joint declaration that calls for both sides to elevate the level of military, security and economic cooperation but saw a low possibility of them clinching a treaty akin to a military alliance.

Putin will arrive in Pyongyang on Tuesday evening and sign "important" documents with the North's leader Wednesday, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as telling reporters by Russia's news agency TASS.
But the deal was scrapped in 1996 after the Soviet Union established diplomatic ties with South Korea in 1990 and collapsed the following year.
It also comes nine months after Kim traveled to Russia's Far East in September last year for a summit with Putin.
In late May, North Korea's attempt to launch a military spy satellite ended in failure as a satellite-carrying rocket exploded right after liftoff.
The North has a desperate need to earn foreign currency due to international sanctions, while Russia has been facing a labor shortage amid its war with Ukraine. (Yonhap)

It also comes nine months after Kim traveled to Russia's Far East in September last year for a summit with Putin. "Several documents will be signed ... and this can be said about a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty," Ushakov said, adding that if it is signed, it would "outline prospects for further cooperation" between the two nations. Pyongyang is accused of providing weapons and munitions to Russia for use in Moscow's war in Ukraine in return for Russia's suspected technical assistance in the development of North Korea's spy satellite program and economic assistance. Analysts said Kim and Putin may adopt a joint declaration that calls for both sides to elevate the level of military, security and economic cooperation but saw a low possibility of them clinching a treaty akin to a military alliance. North Korea and the former Soviet Union signed a treaty of friendship and mutual assistance in 1961, when the North's national founder Kim Il-sung visited Moscow. The treaty included a provision for the so-called automatic military intervention, under which if one side is under an armed attack, the other provides military troops and other aid without hesitation. But the deal was scrapped in 1996 after the Soviet Union established diplomatic ties with South Korea in 1990 and collapsed the following year. In 2000, North Korea and Russia signed a new treaty of bilateral cooperation, but it did not contain such a provision, though it stated that both sides "immediately make contacts" in case one of them faces a crisis of being invaded. Experts said North Korea and Russia are expected to highlight cooperation in the economic sector, as their arms deals and military cooperation constitute a violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions banning Pyongyang's nuclear and missile programs. In an article contributed Tuesday to the Rodong Sinmun, the North's main newspaper, Putin said Russia has a plan to build trade and settlement systems with North Korea that will not be controlled by Western countries. He also said the two nations will pump up exchanges and cooperation in such areas as education, tourism and culture. Experts said Russia is not expected to transfer sensitive weapons technology to North Korea, such as a nuclear-powered submarine, in return for Pyongyang's arms supplies. "What Russia could give the most to North Korea would be to assist its space development program, such as with satellites," Park Won-gon, a professor at Ewha Womans University, said. In late May, North Korea's attempt to launch a military spy satellite ended in failure as a satellite-carrying rocket exploded right after liftoff. In November last year, North Korea successfully placed a spy satellite into orbit, and it has a plan to launch three more such satellites in 2024. The issue of North Korea's dispatch of its workers abroad could also be discussed at the upcoming summit, experts said.
